This was clear evidence of his intent, to sell Blackshades to criminals. All that language that this was only for educational purposes or for a parent to monitor their kid wasn't gonna fly anymore. When you're selling it to criminals on a dark web forum to steal credit card data with, then that’s clear intent. In 2012, the trap snapped shut. The FBI ran a sting operation called Operation Card Shop. It led to twenty-four arrests in eight countries. Almost all of these arrests were for credit card fraud, but there was one exception. One of the people arrested was Michael Hogue, the maker of Blackshades. He was charged under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act for conspiracy to commit computer hacking and transmission of malware. Writing and selling software isn't illegal, but writing and selling software with the intent of logging keystrokes, ransomwaring files, stealing credit cards, and spying on webcams without consent is illegal. Hogue cooperated with investigators, which meant he avoided prison entirely. He was sentenced to five years of probation and he was ordered to forfeit $40,000, and had to perform 500 hours of community service. So, that’s it, right? Co-creator of Blackshades arrested, 2,000 people in cuffs, game over for Blackshades at least, right? Except it wasn't. The Blackshades website stayed up and operational and kept selling it to people for forty bucks. What's hilarious is around that time, Blackshades became so popular that you could find pirated versions of it floating around, too. People who didn't want to pay the $40 could download it and install a pirated version and use it, and it’s hilarious because almost certainly a pirated version of Blackshades is going to come with some other malware bundled on it. You're gonna get some other spy tool installed if you install this. People were spying on the spies. Over the next year, Blackshades did not shrink. It grew. In 2013 Blackshades made its news again. REPORTER: Miss Teen USA 2013, Cassidy Wolf, was one of the victims of a hacker using the malicious software called Blackshades RAT, or remote access tool. Authorities say last year a hacker used Wolf’s personal computer webcam to take nude photos of her and threatened to post them online if Wolf didn't send him more revealing photos. A stranger said he had photos of her, photos taken in her bedroom through her webcam, on her own computer after he hacked into it. He was arrested in this operation, too, and he pleaded guilty. He received a suspended sentence, 200 hours of community service, and seven years on the sex offender registry. The forums are dead. The people who built it got arrested. But even though Blackshades today is mostly a museum piece, malware doesn't really die. It evolves. The $40 RAT with the friendly menu got replaced by newer ones with different names. The criminal economy moved into newer, more sophisticated malware that’s harder to detect. What's still true is malware wants to be sneaky and live quietly. It doesn't want the victim to know they are infected. There’s an asymmetry of knowledge here which is a huge gap, actually. Most people don't know enough about computers or how to secure them to protect themselves reliably, and these attackers rely on that lack of knowledge to hide in the wires, under the radar. Listening to shows like this starts to bridge that gap. Now you're aware that tools like this exist in the world, and they're a big deal. I mean, this one resulted in one of the largest global cyber operations in history. This isn't just some little thing. This is a huge problem. So, awareness is step number one for your safety. Be aware that messages from friends can contain malware, and it doesn't always mean that they sent it to you. It’s always good to verify things out-of-band if you're not sure. Like, if you get a text message from a friend with a suspicious link, call them on the phone and be like, hey, did you just send me this text? [Music] It’s always better to be safe than sorry. Data breaches are extremely common, and malware like this makes it easy for an attacker to get into your computer to see your stuff. So treat your sensitive documents and photos with much more care than normal. For me, I store stuff offline on a hard drive that’s encrypted. It’s a pain in the neck to interact with those files on there, but that’s the point. I want to make it really hard for anyone else to access it, too. There are also USB sticks that you can get which encrypt all the data on it, and to decrypt it you have to enter in a PIN code. Storing stuff on an encrypted USB stick is a pretty good idea, especially since things like mobile phones can't decrypt a hard drive to interact with it. You should treat the internet as a hostile place, because it is. Be very, very cautious when downloading things, clicking links, installing stuff, accepting pop-up options. For me personally, I try to adopt a very minimal approach when it comes to the software and apps I use. The fewer the better, because it reduces the attack surfaces for things that can go wrong. I’m seeing cases these days that have a little slider on the back of the phone so it covers the camera, and I love that. I have one of those myself. But what about the front camera? I haven't seen any cases that cover that. There are little camera covers that you can stick on it, but in my experience, they just always pop off after a few days. I’ve actually experienced with a ton of different types of tape. Electrical tape is easy to peel off for a photo and it doesn't leave much residue, but you need to swap the tape out every month or so or else it gets gooey. I also unplug the TV when I go into hotel rooms when I stay there, since a lot of them have cameras and mics in them, too. Of course you should keep your system and apps updated. Use a different complex password for every service app and website you have an account for. [Music] Actually, I use a different e-mail address for every account that I have as well. This way I immediately know if something doesn't look right because it’ll be for an e-mail that I only use for one thing, and now I’m getting something else from it. It’s not a bad idea to use an antivirus scan every now and then to check for malware on your devices. I’m not gonna plug any here, though, but do some research and find one that’s trusted and reputable. I’m not sure we can achieve perfect privacy or security, but like I’ve said before, when you're trying to secure your stuff, it’s kinda like running from a bear in the woods. You don't need to be faster than the bear; you just need to be faster than your friend who’s also running from the bear in order to stay alive. Your goal is to make it hard for an attacker to get to your stuff so that they just move on to an easier target. Outro: [Outro music] This show is created by me, Papa Ransom, Jack Rhysider. This one was written by motherboard, Yale Grauer. Your kids spend a month begging for an AI toy dog they found online. At $30, marked down 70% from $100, it feels cheap enough to risk, and you finally cave. You know online orders like this can go sideways, but the worst-case scenario is a piece of junk and a few disappointed kids, right?

The dog arrives, and it's basically a battery-operated stuffed animal with no AI inside. You mutter a few curse words under your breath and write it off. What you never see is that your $30 went to one of more than 250 near-identical websites in the same cybercrime network.

Mastercard scam investigators ordered the same dog, aka Wuffy, and followed the money trail. The online store looked legit, with a 4.7-star rating and customer support that answered fast and in detail. But the payment record showed a company headquartered in Lithuania while the site listed a US address, and the store had 250 look-alikes that all carried a 4.7-star rating and a 70% discount. Mastercard's analysis tied an estimated $50 million a year in transactions to the network, and the full scale was likely larger.

Why nobody chases a $30 charge

Victims see the loss, but the trail behind it, who got paid and what that money funded next, stays hidden. A scam like Wuffy is built to keep it that way.

According to Ann Johnson, Mastercard's Executive Vice President of Security Solutions, scammers like credit cards because the loss lands on someone else. When a store turns out to be a scam, the bank covers the loss. Scammers rarely have to pay any of it back, and they know it. So they keep prices reasonable on purpose. They list a $100 "regular" price, so $30 feels like a Black Friday deal. They count on buyers to write off a $30 charge, since fighting it costs more time and money than it's worth.

Now multiply that across more than 250 websites. Each charge looks too small to chase, and only someone who connects the dots across all of them sees the full scale.

For the cybercriminal, a convincing cover story and a price nobody pushes back on add up to steady money with little risk. For you, it's a $30 annoyance that's easy to forget.

Where a $40 million ransom really goes

The criminals behind Wuffy hid in plain sight, making small sales incrementally through a legit-looking store and normal payment systems.

Ransomware has the opposite problem. You're the ransomware gang, and the victim just paid, which leaves you holding millions in traceable crypto. No mainstream exchange will take that much without asking questions, so you need someone who can clean it.

Investigative journalist Geoff White, who covers organized crime and technology, tells the story of one reported $40 million ransom paid by CNA Financial, a US financial firm. As he tells it, Britain's National Crime Agency (NCA), in an investigation called Operation Destabilise, followed the money and traced chunks of it to accounts it links to Ekaterina Zhdanova, a Russian socialite.

"CNA Financial's daily revenues are apparently $38 million. It's a massive amount of money. You can't go to Coinbase or Kraken with that huge quantity of money and expect them not to ask a lot of questions. So the hackers were looking for somewhere else to put that money." - Geoff White, author and investigative journalist

Zhdanova reportedly tried Garantex first, a sanctioned Russian exchange, which only made the crypto hotter. Then she turned to UK drug gangs. The NCA says she offered them a swap: their cash for her crypto. The gangs wanted to unload bulky, vulnerable piles of cash, and crypto could cross borders to buy more product.

"Where does the money from ransomware go? Suddenly you expand out into this massive world connecting all these different networks, not just criminal, but illicit and state-level." - Geoff White

The money trail keeps branching. When Russia invaded Ukraine, Russians with frozen money wanted funds in the UK to buy property or pay school fees. Reportedly, they paid Zhdanova in rubles, and she freed up the same amount in cash in the UK.

The NCA says another branch was tied to the Russian government's efforts to move money into the UK to fund spy rings. Police raided a guest house and found surveillance gear, including a Minion toy with a hidden camera. Six people were convicted, and the NCA says Zhdanova sat at the heart of the funding.

The bottom line is that a company that pays a ransom has no way to know where the money will end up, and neither does anyone who pays $30 for a toy dog.

We can all cut off the money trail

Criminals watch their margins closely, so every bit of friction helps, whether you're protecting your own card or your company's accounts.

If a deal or request is too good to be true, it is. Don't share your information. Take your business elsewhere, to retailers you trust.

If someone contacts you claiming to be your bank or a trusted vendor, stop and verify through a number or website you already know, like the one on the back of your card. Spoofed phone numbers are common, and a link a caller sends can be one digit off.

Talk about scams at home and work, especially with younger family members and colleagues, whose sense of what's private online may differ from yours.

Ready to start following the money trail? Watch the full _declassified episode.

More than 100 stores in several European countries saw their fridges and freezers heat up overnight from Sunday to Monday, and several retailers have blamed a cyberattack. The incidents closely resemble the attacks that disrupted European supermarkets three weeks ago.

The affected businesses, ranging from major chains to small butcher shops, are in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden. Some units were set as high as 50°C (122°F), and problems have also been reported in Finland, Italy and Portugal.

Nobody has taken responsibility for the attacks. Investigators have not established whether the two waves are connected.

The first wave hit France overnight from October 11 to 12. Around 700 supermarkets had their refrigeration units forced into defrost mode, including Intermarché, Carrefour, Coopérative U and Monoprix stores. Food was spoiled, and the attacks reportedly caused fires.

CERT-FR, the incident response team of France’s cybersecurity agency ANSSI, initially linked the compromises to Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC series controllers. A day later, it expanded its alert to cover Copeland and Dixell XWEB systems. Danfoss said most of the hacked units were legacy products it no longer updated.

Exposed Danfoss, Copeland controllers hijacked in new attacks

The technique appears to be the same. Stephan Moelans, CEO of Belgian refrigeration firm Sabcobel, told the Belga news agency that the attackers forced the units’ evaporators into defrost mode, as happened in France.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

According to Moelans, a software update is not enough to fully resolve the weakness, and the affected equipment also needs to be physically modified.

Dutch broadcaster NOS reported that, as far as is known, the targeted devices were made by Danfoss and Copeland. An Estonian refrigeration supplier said the units attacked there were older Danfoss models.

Danfoss said that on October 13 it had told its customers to cut their systems’ internet connections and to reconnect only through a secure network. “Most stores took action at that time, but a small number did not,” a company spokesperson told NOS.

Security researcher Kevin Beaumont said people he spoke with had confirmed that every freezer hit on Monday had a management interface reachable from the internet. According to Beaumont, many of the devices are end-of-life and have no available patch.

Officials have not publicly explained how the attackers got in.

Deception security firm Lupovis told SecurityWeek that, between October 20 and 30, it saw suspicious activity aimed at its Danfoss AK-SM refrigeration controller sensors, including sensors in some of the affected regions. Most of the login attempts relied on factory-default credentials that Danfoss documents publicly, while others appeared to be trying to fingerprint specific Danfoss controller components.

“The activity peaked on 26 October, and importantly, we had not observed this behaviour on these sensors before 20 October. All authentication attempts were rejected by our sensors,” said Lupovis CEO Xavier Bellekens, adding that the timing is noteworthy.

Censys has found just over 1,000 Danfoss StoreView interfaces reachable online worldwide. “France continues to lead Danfoss StoreView exposures globally, followed by Belgium and the US,” the internet intelligence firm said.

The number of exposed StoreView instances in France has fallen sharply, from 1,825 before the October attacks to 220 at the time of Censys’ latest analysis.

By matching firmware build dates, Censys estimates that 41% of the French instances still online run a patched version. It counted 138 exposed instances in Belgium, 51 in the Netherlands and 50 in Sweden, of which 68%, 37% and 58%, respectively, appear to be patched.

Only a handful of exposed instances were seen in Luxembourg, Ireland and Estonia. Censys did not indicate whether any patched devices were among those compromised on Monday.

Belgium among hardest hit

Belgium appears to have taken the biggest hit. Delhaize said an IT incident disrupted refrigeration at several dozen of its stores, Carrefour counted 15 affected locations out of more than 700, and Colruyt said five franchised Spar shops were attacked.

An IKEA store in Mons was hit as well, and the Belgian federal prosecutor’s office has opened an investigation.

In Luxembourg, four Delhaize outlets were affected. In Ireland, SuperValu pulled chilled and frozen products from 13 stores where one specific refrigeration model was impacted.

Swedish grocer ICA confirmed that a limited number of its stores were impacted, while Coop reported problems at a handful of locations. An ICA store manager said they had to throw out significant amounts of food.

In the Netherlands, Danfoss said the systems of at least 17 businesses were hit, mainly butcher shops and small grocers.

Finnish retailer Kesko said a few of its smaller stores had temperature disruptions. In Italy, the operator of several Coop-branded supermarkets in Sicily alerted the national cybersecurity agency, and in Portugal, the Mosqueteiros group confirmed incidents at seven Intermarché stores.

EU agriculture commissioner Christophe Hansen called the attacks a deliberate bid to disrupt the food supply chain and erode consumer trust. “The repeated occurrence of these cyberattacks is deeply concerning,” he said.

Hansen said the bloc’s food security is not under threat for now, but he acknowledged the food that had to be thrown away and the harm to businesses.

NIS2 Article 20 makes management bodies answerable for the access controls they approve, and boards are starting to ask for proof that those controls work.

NIS2 board accountability gives directors a more direct role in cybersecurity. Under Article 20, the management bodies of essential and important entities must approve the cybersecurity risk-management measures required by the directive, oversee their implementation, and can be held liable for infringements, subject to national law.

That obligation is live across most of the EU, with four member states going to the Court of Justice in July for failing to notify full transposition.

Access control is one of the required measures. Directors are not expected to decide who gets administrator rights or review individual user accounts. They do, however, need to know that access is being controlled, that someone has responsibility for managing the risk, and that problems are being addressed.

An estimated 160,000 entities fall within the scope of NIS2 across the EU.

Approval is only part of the job

Article 20 requires management bodies to both approve cybersecurity risk-management measures and oversee their implementation. It also requires the members of those bodies to undergo cybersecurity training, and to offer comparable training to employees on a regular basis.

The measures themselves are set out in Article 21. They include access control policies and asset management, along with the use of multi-factor authentication or continuous authentication solutions where appropriate.

Many organizations have traditionally left these decisions to security and IT teams. Under NIS2, the board still needs to know whether the measures it approved are being implemented.

Day-to-day responsibility can remain with the CISO and IT teams. The difficulty comes when the person responsible for a risk does not control the budget, systems, or people needed to address it.

Greece’s implementation goes further in defining who carries that responsibility. Its NIS2 law requires essential and important entities to appoint a suitably qualified member of their organization as an Information and Communication Systems Security Officer. The officer coordinates compliance, must have the resources needed to do the job, and operates independently of the company’s data protection officer.

Access problems also need to reach the board in terms that it can act on. If an MFA rollout has failed or administrators have more access than they need, the board needs to understand the risk of leaving it unresolved. The CISO may be responsible for the risk without controlling the budget or teams needed to fix it.

The board needs evidence

Board reports often show what the access control policy requires, rather than whether it is being followed.

For example, a company policy will likely require MFA and the removal of accounts when employees leave.

However, the board also needs to know about the exceptions, including old accounts that remain active, excessive privileges, MFA exemptions that have never been reviewed, and suppliers whose access has outlasted their contracts.

The board needs information about how the controls are working in practice.

In a NIS2 access management report from European password and secrets manager Passwork, regulators from two national cybersecurity authorities and independent security leaders describe boards that have absorbed the liability change and now ask for proof that controls work, where they once accepted a summary of the policy.

Organizations should be able to show who can access critical systems, why that access was granted, who approved it, how long it is valid, and when it was changed or revoked. The board needs to know whether that evidence exists and what it says about material access risk.

Personal liability raises the stakes

Implementation is still catching up in parts of Europe. In July 2026, the European Commission referred Ireland, Spain, France, and the Netherlands to the Court of Justice of the European Union for failing to notify full transposition of NIS2 into national law. The Commission also asked the Court to impose financial sanctions.

For organizations in countries where NIS2 has been transposed, regulators have significant enforcement powers.

For essential entities, member states must set a maximum fine of at least €10,000,000 or 2% of the global annual turnover, whichever is higher. Important entities are subject to a lower maximum threshold, of at least €7,000,000 or 1.4% of their global annual turnover, in a similar capacity.

Article 32 also allows competent authorities, in specific circumstances, to seek the temporary prohibition of someone at CEO or legal representative level from exercising managerial functions in an essential entity. This can happen where enforcement action has failed to produce the required response. It is not an automatic consequence of a cyber incident.

Article 20 separately requires member states to ensure that management bodies can be held liable for infringements of Article 21, subject to the applicable rules under national law.

Approving the policy is not the end of the board’s involvement. It also needs information on whether the policy is being followed and what is happening with known problems.

Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report found credential abuse somewhere in the chain of 39% of breaches, more than any other vector. Stolen credentials also circulate at scale, as the exposed database of 24 billion credential records reported in June showed. Directors should expect an answer on which accounts and credentials reach critical systems, who is responsible for them, and whether that access is being controlled.

Give access risk an owner with authority

CISOs briefing their boards should be able to say who owns access-control risk and whether that person has the authority to address it. The board also needs evidence of what is happening.

When an access problem is identified, someone needs to be responsible for getting it fixed. That might mean removing unnecessary privileges or dealing with an MFA exception that has remained in place. If the fix depends on another team’s budget or resources, the board needs to know.

Board reporting should show whether the controls it approved are working, flag significant exceptions that remain unresolved, and who is accountable for closing them.

Google has expanded its Cloud Vulnerability Reward Program (VRP) with a new top-tier reward for high-impact architectural security flaws.

Starting this month, researchers can earn $250,000 for Root-in-Cloud bugs, including tenant-isolation bypasses and complex cross-service logic flaws that let attackers gain full administrative control over arbitrary Google Cloud organizations.

"To earn this premier reward, you must demonstrate full administrative control, the equivalent of 'roles/owner' or complete IAM control, over arbitrary Google Cloud organizations or projects with no prior access or special project setup," said Chris Betz, Google Cloud's Chief Information Security Officer (CISO).

"Additionally, valid vulnerability reports demonstrating remote code execution (RCE) in underlying Google production infrastructure (Borg) or achieving root-in-prod will automatically be evaluated by the Google Cloud VRP panel for root-in-cloud eligibility."

However, to qualify for this reward, the exploits cannot depend on prior access to the victim project, compromised credentials, social engineering, or user interaction.

Additionally, security researchers who achieve execution on Google's production infrastructure must stop probing since escalating, obtaining production credentials, or lateral movement are not allowed and will result in disqualification.

"High incentives require clear, safe rules of engagement. We never want researchers testing exploits against real customer projects," added Cloud VRP Lead Michael Cote.

"Instead, we created a deterministic proof-of-root mechanism using a designated service account. Researchers can cryptographically prove unauthorized access against that identity."

More details on the Google Cloud VRP, including endpoint specifications, JSON payloads, and CLI examples, are available on the rules page.

This follows Google's suspension of submissions to its Open Source Software Vulnerability Rewards Program (OSS VRP) in October after a flood of AI-generated reports.

Google has rewarded thousands of security researchers worldwide with more than $81.6 million since launching its first Vulnerability Reward Program in 2010.

In 2025, Google awarded a record-breaking $17.1 million to over 700 security researchers, a 40% increase from 2024, when it awarded $12 million in total.

AI can find vulnerabilities in minutes, but people still hold the edge in judging what a flaw means for a business. In this Help Net Security interview, Kara Sprague, CEO of HackerOne, talks about business logic bugs, what AI does to the crowd model, and why routine medium-severity findings may pay less.

She also covers the growing pile of AI-assisted submissions, how programs sort useful reports from spam, and which parts of a researcher’s work are hardest to automate, with figures from the 2026 HackerOne Security Research Report.

When an AI system can find a vulnerability in minutes, what is the human hacker still better at, and how long do you expect that to hold?

Humans still have an advantage in judging what a vulnerability means for the organization affected by it. AI can help find more bugs, but deciding which ones deserve attention takes an understanding of how the system is used and what could go wrong.

AI is good at finding familiar types of bugs at scale. It’s less reliable when the weakness depends on how a business operates: a refund process someone can abuse, an approval they can bypass, or several seemingly harmless behaviors that together let them take over an account. Recognizing those problems requires understanding the intended process and imagining how an attacker might use it differently.

Researchers are already shifting their work in that direction. In the 2026 HackerOne Security Research Report, 85% of respondents say they are actively building their AI skills, 68% say AI has pushed them toward more complex bugs with higher bounties, and 72% identify business logic flaws as their fastest-growing category.

I wouldn’t put a date on how long that advantage will last. As models improve, researchers will need to keep adapting how they use them and where they focus their efforts. Understanding the organization, assessing the consequences of a flaw, and making a defensible recommendation about what to fix will remain a substantial part of the work.

HackerOne built its business on the idea that many eyes find more bugs. If machines become some of those eyes, does the crowd model get stronger or does it start to look like a legacy approach?

AI makes the crowd model stronger, although it reduces the value of routine findings.

The benefit of “many eyes” has always been the different perspectives researchers bring. People have different skills and different ideas about how to attack a system. Adding more models doesn’t necessarily offer the same variety, especially when they’re trained on similar data and asked to examine the same targets.

Paying researchers for valid findings still works when they use AI. We have seen researcher payouts rise 26% year over year in the first half of 2026 and accelerate further in the third quarter. There’s also more to investigate. According to the research, the number of programs with AI assets in scope doubled in two years, while valid AI vulnerability reports rose 222%.

Routine, pattern-based findings will become harder to earn money from. As automated tools make those bugs easier to find, programs have less reason to pay researchers to report them.

The case for the crowd still rests on people who approach a problem differently and find something others missed. AI helps them do that work and its ability to produce more findings makes their judgment about which ones matter more valuable.

Bounty payouts reward scarcity. If AI makes routine findings abundant, what happens to the price of a medium-severity bug?

Routine medium-severity bugs will likely earn less. Findings that take deeper investigation and judgment may hold their value or earn more.

Programs pay bounties to reduce risk. If AI makes a familiar type of bug cheaper to find, programs have less reason to offer the same reward. Researchers also face more competition to submit it first. That lowers their chances of getting paid even when the advertised bounty hasn’t changed.

The bug bounty platforms are showing signs of this shift. Since January 2025, submissions have grown 2.8 times, while valid reports have grown 1.9 times. Programs are paying more for critical and novel findings and less, or nothing, for low-severity issues, duplicates, and findings that can be automated. Total payouts have still increased.

But cheaper discovery also helps attackers, which could make leaving a medium-severity vulnerability unfixed more costly. Fixing the problems already reported remains a challenge, with about 70% of security leaders say validated findings reach their backlog faster than their teams can address them. As reports become more plentiful, more of the value lies in confirming the risk and helping teams resolve it.

Program owners already complain about low-quality reports. How much of the AI-generated submission volume you see is useful, and how much is noise that a triager has to wade through?

I can’t give you a reliable split. It’s difficult to tell whether a report was written by a person, generated by a model, or developed using both. Many good reports now involve AI. We can measure the overall volume and the results.

Bug bounty platforms have seen submissions grow 2.8 times since January 2025, while valid reports have grown 1.9 times. We’re receiving more valid findings than ever, but they make up a smaller share of submissions. Most of the other reports are duplicates, informative, out of scope, or spam. A growing share is also awaiting more information from the researchers or a final decision from the program.

Those numbers don’t tell us how much of either increase comes from AI. For programs reviewing reports, the question is whether the evidence demonstrates real security impact. AI makes it easy to produce a convincing-looking report, but checking its claims can still take considerable time.

Programs are responding with submission limits based on researchers’ track records and private access tiers. They also need to get through reviews faster. That will take both people and automation; otherwise, useful findings will spend longer waiting alongside reports that don’t warrant action.

Which parts of a researcher’s work do you believe are hardest to automate: creativity in chaining flaws, understanding business logic, or something else? What is your evidence?

I’d put business logic first, followed by chaining vulnerabilities into an attack.

Chaining involves searching for ways that weaknesses can work together, and models are getting better at that. Business logic depends more on understanding what a system is supposed to allow. The code may not tell you why a refund needs approval, who should be able to authorize a payment, or when an exception creates an opportunity for abuse. A model can help test those situations, but someone needs to provide the relevant context. Knowing which details matter takes experience.

The evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive. 72% of researcher respondents identify business logic flaws as their fastest-growing vulnerability category. That tells us where researchers are finding opportunities; it doesn’t establish how long humans will retain an advantage over models.

I’d also include the judgment involved in deciding which findings need attention now. In the same report, 58% of security leaders say product delivery or business priorities delay fixes for critical and high-severity vulnerabilities. Resolving those competing demands takes discussion with the people responsible for the product and a clear understanding of the consequences. Someone has to take responsibility for the decision.

Apple warns German Bundestag lawmakers of mercenary spyware attacks; BSI urges victims to assume compromise.

The German government is warning politicians and public figures that they were targeted by government-backed spyware. The warning follows Apple’s notifications, which began reaching iPhones on October 29, according to the federal cybersecurity office, the BSI. The BSI says members of the Bundestag and other notable people got an Apple alert about an attack with so-called mercenary spyware.

“The Federal Office for Information Security ( BSI ) has learned that several members of the German Bundestag and other public figures have received a threat notification from Apple on their devices since October 29, 2026. In the notification, Apple states that it has detected an attack using so-called mercenary spyware . This is commercially developed, advanced spyware that has frequently been used in the past by state actors against specific, targeted individuals.” reads the notice issued by BSI.

“The BSI (Federal Office for Information Security) is unaware whether these notifications indicate actual compromises or merely signal attempted attacks.y “

“Germany’s digital minister, Karsten Wildberger, has confirmed that members of the Bundestag and the federal government received warnings from Apple that their iPhones may have been targeted by spyware.” states the report.

Digital minister Karsten Wildberger confirmed it on ARD’s Bericht aus Berlin on Sunday, saying there had been “a notification from Apple that certain devices may have been compromised” and that members of both the Bundestag and the federal government were among those warned. Digital minister said the BSI had reacted super quickly and written to everyone affected. Wildberger didn’t say how many politicians got the alerts or who they are.

“According to Wildberger, the BSI advised those affected to assume – as a precaution – that their device may have been compromised, because the alerts do not show whether an attack succeeded.” states Euronews.

The German government has not revealed who was targeted. Government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius told the Financial Times that officials are taking the incident and Apple’s warning very seriously. However, he did not say which government members received the alerts or whether Chancellor Friedrich Merz was among them. Apple has not commented on the reports, according to Euronews.

The Apple warning does not provide all the answers. Apple does not identify the governments behind these attacks, nor does it confirm whether a device was actually infected. Germany’s cybersecurity agency, the BSI, also says it is unclear whether the alerts indicate successful infections or only attempted attacks.

Apple says mercenary spyware is far more advanced than common cybercrime tools and that most users will never be targeted. This commercial surveillance software is often used on behalf of governments to spy on specific individuals. It can infect devices through so-called zero-click attacks, which do not require victims to open a message or click a link. In most cases, victims do not notice anything unusual.

Once a phone is compromised, the BSI says, attackers can read messages, including in encrypted apps, and access calls, contacts, calendars and location. They can also turn on the camera and microphone. That’s the whole phone, not a corner of it.

For recipients the BSI’s advice is concrete. Update the operating system immediately, unless you plan a forensic analysis, and consider turning on Lockdown Mode, which makes new attacks harder but doesn’t remove an existing infection. Lockdown Mode limits some features such as message attachments, link previews and FaceTime calls from unknown people, while calls and plain text messages keep working.

If the risk looks high, the BSI suggests replacing the device. That means resetting every account used on it and, to make repeat attacks harder, changing the phone number. Then set a new device passcode, change the passwords of your Apple account and email, and make sure two-factor authentication is on.

The BSI recommends turning on Signal’s registration lock and WhatsApp’s two-step verification, with a new PIN for each. It also advises removing any linked devices you don’t recognize.

Anyone who received a warning can email the BSI Service Center at service-center@bsi.bund.de. This helps the agency work out how many people may be affected. The agency says a genuine Apple warning never asks you to click links, open files, install apps or profiles, or share passwords and codes. These warnings appear on the lock screen, in settings, by email and at the top of account.apple.com after you sign in.

The warnings weren’t limited to Germany. Beirut-based filmmaker Radwan Mortada said on X that Apple had warned him about another attack against his device. He had already been targeted by spyware in 2021.

Affected individuals were urged to contact the BSI directly .”

Hackers who breached Harvard University's Alumni Affairs and Development systems in November 2025 stole data linked to more than 850,000 unique email addresses, according to breach notification service Have I Been Pwned.

Harvard is a private Ivy League research university with over 20,000 faculty and staff, over 24,500 undergraduate and graduate students, and more than 400,000 alumni worldwide.

As the university discovered on November 18, 2025, the attackers gained access to the personal information of students, alumni, donors, staff, and faculty members, including email addresses, telephone numbers, home and business addresses, event attendance records, donation details, and "biographical information pertaining to University fundraising and alumni engagement activities."

However, Klara Jelinkova, Harvard's Vice President and University Chief Information Officer (CIO), said the breached IT systems didn't store Social Security numbers, passwords, payment card information, or financial information.

Although Harvard has not attributed the attack to a specific hacking group or threat actor, the ShinyHunters extortion gang claimed responsibility and said it stole over 1 million records containing identifiable information and donation data after breaching the university's systems.

The cybercriminals then leaked a 1.1GB archive of documents on their dark web leak site in early February after Harvard refused to pay a ransom to have the stolen data returned and destroyed.

​While a Harvard spokesperson could not share how many individuals had their information exposed when BleepingComputer reached out at the time for more details, Have I Been Pwned analyzed the data leaked by the cybercrime gang and confirmed on Tuesday that the breach exposed the data of 850,500 accounts, including names, email addresses, dates of birth, phone numbers, physical addresses, social media profiles, and more

"The data contained 851k unique email addresses relating to the university's alumni and fundraising systems, along with extensive profile information for donors, alumni, parents and some faculty, staff and students," it said.

Two other Ivy League schools, Princeton University and the University of Pennsylvania, disclosed data breaches in November 2025, both confirming that the attackers accessed donors' information.

In October 2025, Harvard also told BleepingComputer that it was investigating a second data breach after the Clop ransomware gang claimed that it had breached the university's systems using an Oracle E-Business Suite (EBS) zero-day vulnerability.

Two months later, the University of Phoenix (UoPX) joined the list of US universities breached by Clop using the same Oracle EBS flaw and revealed that the ransomware gang stole data from nearly 3.5 million UoPX students, staff, and suppliers in August 2025.

8a58dc8719f7.text:
Composer 2.11 has introduced dependency cooldowns, giving PHP developers a native way to delay newly published package versions before they become eligible for installation. The release arrives nearly a year after developers first requested the feature, bringing Composer into line with package managers that have already adopted minimum release age policies to reduce exposure to supply chain attacks.

The new config.policy.cooldown setting allows developers to specify a waiting period in hours, days, or weeks. It is disabled by default and applies during dependency resolution, including composer update and composer require. Existing lockfile installations remain unaffected.

The feature also supports organization-wide configuration through Private Packagist, which can enforce cooldowns regardless of the Composer version developers and CI systems are running.

Preventing Cooldown Bypasses #

The original GitHub issue opened in November 2025 and gained urgency following a series of high-profile supply chain compromises. An initial implementation was submitted in December, but the feature missed Composer 2.10 as the maintainers worked through how to enforce cooldowns reliably.

In May, after additional attacks affected Packagist, developers pressed the maintainers for an update. Composer co-founder Nils Adermann explained that the feature was being held up by changes needed to make release metadata trustworthy.

The existing time field in Composer package metadata could be derived from a Git commit date or supplied through composer.json. Both are under the publisher's control, allowing an attacker to backdate a malicious release and bypass a cooldown.

Packagist introduced a new published-time field in June, recording when a version first became available through the registry. Composer 2.11 now uses that timestamp rather than trusting dates supplied by package publishers. Repositories without the required metadata cause dependency resolution to fail unless an explicit fallback is configured.

The cooldown feature is part of a broader security effort by Composer and Packagist. In a May security update, maintainers specifically cited the April compromise of intercom/intercom-php, and the May attack on Laravel Lang among recent incidents affecting the PHP ecosystem. The update outlined several security initiatives, including malware detection, version immutability, and the planned cooldown policy.

Cooldowns Are Now Standard Across Package Ecosystems #

For years, dependency management favored staying on the latest compatible releases. That assumption is changing. With compromised packages appearing on a regular basis, living on the bleeding edge has become considerably less appealing. Cooldowns are increasingly treated as standard supply chain security practice, and some package managers have already made them the default.

Composer is joining a movement already well underway across JavaScript, Ruby, Python, and Rust tooling.

pnpm introduced minimum release ages in September 2025 and made a 24-hour delay the default in version 11. Yarn has also enabled a release-age gate by default, while npm and Bun offer configurable delays. GitHub introduced a three-day default cooldown for Dependabot version updates in July.

In Ruby, Bundler added cooldown support in June, and gem.coop began testing registry-level delays earlier this year. Cargo is next, with minimum publish age support scheduled to become stable in Rust 1.100 on November 12.

Unlike pnpm and Yarn, Composer is leaving the feature opt-in, a decision its maintainers debated during development over concerns about disrupting existing workflows.

Composer also deliberately avoids automatically exempting security fixes. The maintainers rejected that approach because an attacker with publishing access could potentially create an advisory or exploit an existing one to get a malicious release through the cooldown. Developers can use --no-cooldown to install an urgent fix immediately without disabling other security policies. Composer also supports permanent exemptions for specific packages through the cooldown policy's ignore setting.

Security fixes still demand quick updates, especially as AI-assisted vulnerability disclosures accelerate, but for routine dependency updates, cooldowns are becoming best practice. Composer's implementation arrives later than many of its peers, but its adoption adds another major ecosystem to the shift toward giving new dependencies time to be examined before installation.

e5842bc0d6c4.text:
AI agents are transforming enterprise computing. What began with employees using AI assistants is evolving into autonomous agents that access enterprise resources, invoke tools, execute code, and take action at machine speed.

This introduces a new security and safety challenge. Organizations must protect agents from attacks while ensuring those agents operate safely and as intended. Security teams need to discover where agents operate, understand what they were instructed to do, trace their actions, and intervene when their behavior becomes dangerous.

Traditional security approaches provide only part of the picture. Endpoint runtime security monitors execution but lacks the AI-specific context needed to explain what triggered it. Network inspection can monitor AI communications but not the actions that agents take on systems. Agent-level integrations can inspect AI interactions but cannot reveal downstream execution.

At Fal.Con Europe 2026, CrowdStrike unveiled innovations that advance AI detection and response (AIDR) across three critical dimensions: architecture, coverage, and controls. We also introduced a new AI kill switch for CrowdStrike Falcon® Guardian that empowers security teams to rapidly cut off AI model access at AI gateways when agents become dangerous. And we shared the general availability of CrowdStrike Falcon® Complete for Guardian, which extends 24/7 managed detection and response to AI security.

The Right Architecture for Securing AI Agents

Securing AI agents requires visibility and control across three critical layers: OS-level runtime execution, network communications, and agent interactions. Falcon Guardian brings these layers together to connect what agents are instructed to do with what they execute.

OS-level runtime security is the foundation (Available now): The Falcon sensor provides deep visibility into agents’ activity, including the processes they launch, commands they run, and resources they access. This visibility is not achievable directly via network inspection or per-agent hook integration approaches.

Endpoint network inspection extends visibility into agent communications (Pre-beta): CrowdStrike announced plans to expand this capability to macOS, where it will inspect traffic entering and leaving the endpoint to help security teams identify risky interactions.

Agent-level hooks provide direct inspection and policy enforcement within supported AI agents (Available now): Hooks for Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, OpenCode, and Cursor enable organizations to inspect prompts and block malicious activity at the source, before harmful actions are executed.

Together, these three layers give Falcon Guardian visibility into agent instructions, communications, and runtime execution. CrowdStrike® Agent Graph connects this activity, linking what agents were instructed to do with what they actually executed and the resources they affected. This gives security teams the context to understand agent behavior, investigate threats, and trace their impact from prompt to process.

See it in action:

The Right Coverage: Secured AI Wherever It Operates

Falcon Guardian initially focused on securing workforce AI adoption and autonomous agents at the endpoint, where employees interact with AI and agents execute with user permissions.

Now, as enterprises build and deploy their own agents in production environments, CrowdStrike is expanding Falcon Guardian's AI-specific protections across more of the cloud infrastructure the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform already secures. Newly announced capabilities will extend Falcon Guardian coverage across Linux, cloud workloads, Kubernetes, and managed AI platforms.

Expanded cloud coverage (Pre-beta): On Linux, Falcon Guardian will bring agent discovery, visibility, and AI-specific detections to Claude Code and OpenAI Codex. In cloud workloads and Kubernetes, Falcon Guardian will extend these capabilities to enterprise-developed AI agents and applications, including those built with LangChain and LangGraph. Using the Falcon Linux sensor, deployed directly or as a Kubernetes DaemonSet, Falcon Guardian will connect AI activity with surrounding runtime, workload, and identity context.

For provider-managed AI environments, Falcon Guardian will expand agent discovery and AI-layer visibility, beginning with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. This will help security teams identify managed agents, understand their components and interactions, and assess AI-specific risks without requiring access to provider-controlled infrastructure.

601a270f88ff.text:
I am delighted to announce CrowdStrike’s intent to acquire Fiddler at Fal.Con EU 2026. Fiddler, a leader in AI observability, will help ensure enterprise AI agents act as intended with pre-deployment evaluation and continuous behavioral monitoring as part of the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform.

Every business deploying AI agents asks the same questions: What are our agents doing? Are they staying on task? Are they acting in a way that could put the business at risk?

AI agents don’t have to be compromised to be dangerous. Those that stay within their guardrails can make a bad decision or take harmful action using valid credentials and approved enterprise tools. Businesses must be able to trace agents’ activity and explain anomalies as these concerns become top of mind among auditors, regulators, board members, and risk managers.

Enterprise AI safety requires a comprehensive approach: Evaluate agents before deployment, understand their decisions and actions, and continuously monitor their behavior. AI observability provides a lens into agent behavior before and after they ship. AI explainability shows why agents made their decisions and where their actions may have gone awry.

Fiddler delivers both. It will become part of the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform as CrowdStrike Falcon® Observe, generally available in Q4 FY27. With this acquisition, CrowdStrike will extend our AI security capabilities beyond protecting AI systems into proving businesses can safely use AI agents every day.

Building AI Trust in the Agentic Enterprise

Unlike traditional software, AI agents can make autonomous decisions, invoke tools, and take actions across enterprise systems. If software can act autonomously, security needs a record of those actions: what each agent decided, how it acted, what it changed, and the tools it used. They must know whether the agent made the correct decisions to follow its intended task.

As an example: Consider an AI agent using approved tools and valid credentials to process a customer refund. The agent makes an incorrect decision and approves a refund that violates company policy. Traditional security controls may see legitimate activity, but AI explainability reveals why the agent made that decision and where its behavior went wrong.

Fiddler provides AI observability for the agentic era. It helps organizations identify misaligned agents before they are deployed and continues to monitor agent behavior post-deployment so businesses have full visibility into what they’re doing and why.

Before deployment, teams can compare prompts, models, and configurations to evaluate whether agents perform intended tasks safely and accurately before they reach production.

After deployment, teams can trace agents’ decisions and reasoning paths across the full agent hierarchy to detect issues like behavioral drift and unintended actions before they cause harm. Fiddler reconstructs the agent’s decision-making process so teams can trace each failure to the step that caused it.

Fiddler supports auditable AI governance across organizations’ existing agents and tools. Its granular view of agents’ decision-making covers first-party and third-party agents across the enterprise so teams have the data they need to support compliance and audits. Businesses also gain explainability across the frameworks they run, as Fiddler enables teams to instrument agents through OpenTelemetry and supports LangGraph, Amazon Bedrock, AWS Strands, and Google ADK.

As part of the Falcon platform, Fiddler will connect AI agent intent and behavior with Falcon security telemetry across endpoints, identity, cloud, and runtime environments. This will help security teams understand why an agent took an action and what happened across the enterprise as a result. By connecting agent decisions with enterprise security context, CrowdStrike will provide visibility that goes beyond standalone AI observability.

CrowdStrike Delivers the Enterprise AI Control Plane

This milestone extends CrowdStrike’s leadership in protecting the agentic enterprise. Our acquisition of Fiddler, together with CrowdStrike Falcon® Guardian innovations announced today, will bring comprehensive AI security and safety solutions to the Falcon platform.

CrowdStrike can already establish AI agents as trusted identities, connect those identities to the humans operating them, grant access to business systems based on real-time risk, and secure AI agents at runtime. Fiddler will extend the Falcon platform to the earliest stages of the agent lifecycle, before deployment, to monitor their behavior before and after production, and explain the decisions they make.

Falcon Guardian protects AI agents from attacks and misuse. Falcon Observe evaluates and explains whether agents behave as intended. Together, they secure AI operations in the agentic enterprise.

Forward-Looking Statements

This blog contains forward-looking statements, including statements regarding the closing and benefits of the proposed acquisition. These statements involve risks and uncertainties, and actual results may differ materially. There are a number of risks that could cause actual results to differ materially, including the satisfaction of the acquisition’s closing conditions, our ability to integrate Fiddler, and other risks described in the filings we make with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission from time to time.

One Kill Switch with Comprehensive Enforcement Points

Coming soon, CrowdStrike will extend AI Kill Switch beyond gateway enforcement to deliver coordinated agent containment across the Falcon platform.

AI agents operate across endpoints, cloud environments, SaaS applications, browsers, and enterprise identities, often spanning multiple environments in a single chain of activity. When an agent goes rogue, stopping it shouldn't require security teams to investigate and respond separately in every environment.

CrowdStrike's vision is one AI Kill Switch coordinating response across multiple enforcement points. This will bring together the security capabilities of the Falcon platform and its broader ecosystem to contain rogue agents wherever they operate, including:

Endpoint agents: Terminate rogue agents and associated processes directly on affected endpoints and prevent them from restarting.

Cloud agents: Contain or terminate compromised agents operating in cloud environments.

User and agent identities: Leverage CrowdStrike Falcon® Next-Gen Identity Security to revoke agent permissions at runtime and restrict access to enterprise resources.

SaaS agents: Extend containment through CrowdStrike Falcon® Shield to restrict or terminate agent activity within SaaS environments.

Browser sessions: Leverage CrowdStrike Falcon® Seraphic® Enterprise Browser to terminate sessions and disrupt unauthorized activity through web applications.

This evolution will enable increasingly targeted containment so security teams can stop individual rogue agents or groups of agents with surgical precision while minimizing disruption to business operations.

CrowdStrike's architectural advantage goes beyond individual enforcement mechanisms. CrowdStrike® Agent Graph connects AI intent to downstream execution, revealing what an agent was asked to do, what it did, and which systems or resources were affected. This context helps security teams understand the threat and determine where to intervene. CrowdStrike Charlotte Agentic SOAR provides the no-code security orchestration, automation, and response (SOAR) capabilities to coordinate enforcement across the Falcon platform, enabling automated AI Kill Switch workflows triggered by AI-specific detections or risky agent behavior.

Rather than responding to isolated events through disconnected tools, security teams will be able to coordinate containment across the agentic attack surface.

Secure AI Adoption Without Losing Control

AI agents are becoming a powerful part of enterprise operations. As their autonomy and reach expand, organizations need security that can keep pace.

With AI Kill Switch, CrowdStrike introduces a decisive new way to rapidly disrupt dangerous AI activity when risk emerges. This is the first step toward broader enforcement to coordinate containment across the endpoints, identities, cloud environments, SaaS applications, and browsers where agents operate.

The objective is simple: Give organizations the confidence to embrace AI, control its expanding attack surface, and stop threats before they become breaches.

When Claude Cowork executes code locally, it runs inside an isolated virtual machine on the user's computer. On the host, that VM runs as a single opaque process: The agent's activity inside the VM, including the processes it spawns, the packages it installs, and the network connections it makes, is not visible to the host's endpoint security sensor. Because host folders can be mounted into the VM, sensitive data can sit within the agent's reach.

Today at Fal.Con Europe 2026, CrowdStrike announced it is bringing CrowdStrike Falcon® Guardian protection natively into Anthropic's Claude Cowork. Built in partnership with Anthropic in response to enterprise customer demand, this integration extends Falcon protection to AI agents across their lifecycle, from agent creation through job execution. It runs the Falcon sensor directly inside the Cowork VM on both macOS and Windows to bring runtime visibility and detection into the agent's execution environment.

The integration is now available in beta on macOS, with Windows support expected later in November.

How It Works

Consider this scenario: A user asks Cowork for a script to align their slides to a brand standard. While completing the task, the agent installs the latest version of a common Python package. Neither the user nor the agent knows that an adversary has compromised the package at its source. Once installed, that package reads host data through a mounted folder and sends it out to a known malicious endpoint. The Falcon sensor running inside the VM would detect it. This is exactly the type of malicious activity and potential data exfiltration the integration is built to detect as agents execute tasks.

CrowdStrike’s sensor integration with the Cowork VM will deliver:

Visibility and detection where agents execute: Process, package, and network activity inside the Cowork VM will no longer be a blind spot, so teams can detect and investigate threats with the same Falcon telemetry they use everywhere else.

The same visibility on macOS and Windows: The VM runs the same Linux environment on both, so customers get consistent coverage regardless of the OS.

Deployment and control through the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform: Admins will turn the integration on through their existing device management, the same way they deploy the Falcon sensor today, and the Falcon Linux sensor deploys inside the Cowork VM. From there, the team controls it through the Falcon platform so Claude Cowork comes under the same security control plane as the rest of the environment.

Built with Anthropic

CrowdStrike and Anthropic worked together to bring Falcon protection directly into Claude Cowork's execution environment. Anthropic enabled Falcon deployment within Cowork, while CrowdStrike engineered and tested the integration across installation, real-time protection, and ongoing updates. Through this beta integration, enterprises can extend the security they already trust from the Falcon platform to AI agents in Claude Cowork, alongside the virtual machine, permissions, and admin controls built into Cowork.

CrowdStrike’s Architectural Difference

AI agents don't operate in one layer, and neither does Falcon Guardian. Agents reach out over the network to communicate with LLMs, but they also execute processes locally on the workstations where they’re installed. These actions may never cross network boundaries. The Falcon sensor and Falcon Guardian see both agentic workstreams and fuse them together in a single view from CrowdStrike’s endpoint network inspection and OS-level visibility. This unified view, CrowdStrike® Agent Graph, shows analysts not only what agents were asked to do, but what they did at runtime.

CrowdStrike also delivers agent-level enforcement controls via hook integrations for agents such as Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, OpenCode, and Cursor.

The Claude Cowork integration extends Falcon Guardian coverage to a new place agents work. It takes Falcon Guardian’s runtime security foundation into the VM where Cowork runs its code, providing visibility and detection for what the agent executes, installs, and connects to across its lifecycle, from agent creation through job execution.

What's Next

Endpoint agents like Claude Cowork run their code inside a VM that host-only security can't see into. By running the Falcon Linux sensor inside the Cowork VM on macOS and Windows, this integration will close that gap. It will bring Falcon visibility and detection to where agents execute, it will be deployed and controlled through Falcon, and it will extend the runtime foundation of the three layers of AI security in Falcon Guardian.

The integration is focused on visibility and detection inside the VM. Available in beta on macOS, with Windows support expected later in November 2026, it enables customers to deploy the Falcon Linux sensor inside the Cowork VM through their existing device management tools. Their teams gain visibility and detection across the processes, packages, and network activity inside the VM.

Forward-Looking Statements

43a5fb7b5a6c.text:
A password spray is a familiar attack: try a few common passwords against many accounts and hope one works. In October 2026, Wiz Research watched one where the median gap between attempts was exactly one second. Sessions ran for 24 to 30 hours, and blocked addresses were replaced within minutes. No person types like that. The pattern comes from an AI agent, and it points to a tool called ARTEX.

What ARTEX is and who is using it

ARTEX is an open-source framework that runs a penetration test on its own. An operator names a target and a goal, and the agents plan and carry out the steps. Since late August, Google's Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant have seen it used in incident response cases, by extortion groups and suspected espionage operators alike. Microsoft tracks one of those campaigns as Storm-0940. The developer stopped offering the code openly in October, but it had already been copied more than 12,000 times.

The techniques are old, and the time between them is gone

None of what the agent did is new: password spraying, abusing password-reset pages, stolen cloud keys, moving from one system to the next. Google puts it this way: "LLM-enabled offensive tooling does not fundamentally change the techniques attackers use. It reduces the time required to combine them."

The time is the difference. Google reports that one actor typically went from a first compromised account to deep access in about four hours, and once in 15 minutes. Individual steps ran in bursts of seconds: 27 events in 23 seconds while the agent tested what a stolen cloud key could do.

Three gaps, crossed in seconds

This is where the three detection gaps in my whitepaper show up in real incidents. In several cases, the operators handed ARTEX credentials they had already stolen. The agent then logged in with them, so authentication succeeds, and the record of who did what shows ordinary sign-ins (Gap 2). It also reused features that were already there, such as a business application's own notification system to email more than 1,300 employees, so nothing looks wrong (Gap 1). And it crossed from directories to cloud storage to identity services, which separate teams and tools usually watch, so movement isn't visible (Gap 3).

A human operator crossing those boundaries leaves slow, spread-out evidence. An agent leaves the same evidence compressed into minutes, in a window that three separate tickets may never connect.

The pace is the clue, but spotting it does not stop the objective

The speed is also the most readable signal. A one-second rhythm, a permission test every second or so, and a burst of 27 events in 23 seconds stand out once someone looks at timing and sequence together instead of one event at a time.

But Google makes a harder point: detection and response are different jobs, and "simply detecting the attack in time does little to hinder objective completion." If an agent can reach deep access in 15 minutes, an alert that becomes a ticket for the next morning arrives after the objective is complete. The speed of the response has to match the speed of the attacker.

The noisy version is the early version

Google describes current use as early-stage: open-source tools used carelessly, producing campaigns that are broad and noisy but still successful. Its own estimate is that quieter, fully autonomous attacks follow within three to six months. That is a forecast, not an observation. If it holds, the clues above are the easy version, and the window to build timing-based detection and a faster response is open now.

Where Vectra AI fits

At Vectra AI, this is the problem our detection work is built around: a sign-in that the audit log records as a success, followed by behavior that doesn't match the identity that signed in. Google's defensive guidance ends on the same point, that detecting behavioral change depends on seeing identity, cloud, and network activity as one sequence. An agent moving at this pace will cross all three before separate tools finish alerting.

The Mind Your Gaps in the Age of AI-Powered Attacks whitepaper walks through the three detection gaps end to end. Its sections on Gap 1 (nothing looks wrong), Gap 2 (authentication succeeds) and Gap 3 (movement isn't visible) cover the pattern described here.

e3eea1d2b551.text:
Attackers were definitely testing our cybersecurity best practices during Cybersecurity Awareness Month. A cloud region was knocked offline in Japan. Grocery stores across the US and Europe were either taken offline temporarily or lost produce. An AI agent chained two vulnerabilities to breach an organization that was established to help others with vulnerability disclosure. And finally, there were well over one thousand vulnerability patches in a single day. No seriously. Vulnerability management was like walking into a burning building in October.

With that, let’s dive into this month’s security news.

Oct. 7: Ransomware takes down Japanese cloud infrastructure

A Japanese SoftBank subsidiary called IDC Frontier confirmed a ransomware attack began on October 7, impacting nearly 500 companies and local governments.

Allegedly, customers saw messages claiming 3.6PB of data was encrypted in seven minutes.

The ransomware group claims to have deleted snapshots.

This was in addition to other large-scale attacks across the country in October, including Burger King Japan, Nikkei, and Capcom.

Shared responsibility includes your own backups. Test restoring them somewhere that isn’t your provider.

Oct. 11: Hackers burn French fridges

Overnight, between October 11 and 12, hackers forced refrigerators in hundreds of grocery stores across France into continuous defrost mode.

For six hours, the refrigeration equipment was pushed to temperatures of 50°C (122°F).

The Danish manufacturer, Danfoss, said the stores were running outdated firmware or had reached end-of-life support, which left equipment exposed to the internet.

This caused fires and potentially tens of millions of dollars in spoiled food. Although the incident was due to operational equipment exposure, it’s a global wake-up call to the physical impact of supply chain attacks.

Oct. 20-21: Six Linux vulnerabilities dropped at once

Trend Micro’s Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) sent five Linux kernel reports to the Linux kernel security team and one report to the ConnMan mailing list, all of which went out to the broader public mailing lists.

ZDI-CAN-33367 is a local privilege escalation in skb_zerocopy() with a public proof of concept. It’s another gap in the Dirty Frag fix (CVE-2026-43284) from May.

Oct. 21: PHP2Shell

PHP shipped two emergency releases on October 21 for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

An unauthenticated attacker can run code with HTTP requests alone, and researchers estimate 1.3 -1.9 million exposed hosts are potentially vulnerable.

Exploitation started before the patches existed. Amazon reported seeing an attempt on October 17. Organizations need to patch immediately, restart every PHP worker, and assume breach as they scan environments for signs of unauthorized access.

Oct. 21: Node2Shell

Node2Shell, also known as HTTP2Shell, landed on organizations’ radars after Node.js fixed an out-of-bounds write in its bundled Brotli decoder on October 21.

The first public GitHub repository tracking the CVE appeared only hours after the fix, and exploitation attempts were confirmed within days.

The decoder also ships in Bun, Python Brotli packages, and some Envoy configurations.

Additional Sysdig TRT findings

An AI agent chained two vulnerabilities to exploit a vulnerability disclosure program

On October 2, Sysdig TRT published an initial blog on the breach of the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) on September 21.

The attacker exploited two vulnerabilities in the Zammad open source helpdesk tool. These were identified as CVE-2026-102489, a remote code execution flaw, and CVE-2026-102490, a local privilege escalation flaw.

Originally thought to be zero-days, Zammad said it received a report on CVE-2026-102489 in August, before the breach.

Pickle bypasses

On October 27, the Sysdig TRT published an analysis on using pickles to bypass model-loading defenses in machine learning.

Six documented CVE bypasses beat PyTorch weights_only, Keras safe_mode, and picklescan. The check and the loader disagreed about what the file was in each case.

Loading a pickle file executes the code inside it. That’s a design flaw, not a patchable bug, so the fix is in the formatting. Switch to safetensors where possible and use runtime to detect what happens after the pickle is loaded.

Also in the news

Microsoft patches a record 1,411 flaws: Vulnerability discovery is quickly outpacing security teams’ capability to remediate. KrebsOnSecurity said the prior month’s record of 972 patched flaws was 10 times a “normal” Microsoft patch load, and October dwarfed it. The increase is due to the internal use of AI platforms to find vulnerabilities within Microsoft products. Security teams need to prioritize reachability and exploitation. This month included one actively exploited zero-day (CVE-2026-96951), two publicly disclosed ones, and 70 critical flaws.

US and European grocery store operations disrupted: Ahold Delhaize confirmed a cybersecurity incident on October 12 after taking systems offline on October 11 to contain it. Albert Heijn, Etos, Gall & Gall, Delhaize, and Stop & Shop were some of the stores affected.

Nation-state threat actors using agentic AI: China-affiliated threat group Storm-0940 used agents to compromise ConnectWise customers, according to Microsoft on October 21. The group used the open source ARTEX framework to attempt sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants. In multiple cases, the actors moved from targeting to privileged cloud access in less than three hours.

Closing thoughts

Look at the clocks from this month. PHP2Shell was exploited four days before the patch. There was a PoC in a public repo for Node2Shell within hours. Storm-0940 went from targeting to privileged cloud access in under three hours. Patch what’s reasonable first, in a reasonable amount of time. But watch for what happens after an exploit is known. Attackers can’t hide behavior.

And we just wrapped Cybersecurity Awareness Month. If you want to take a breather and step away from vulnerabilities for just a moment, here’s a list of simple things you should be doing daily to avoid a breach.

To stay informed between our monthly wrap-ups, you can get the latest from the Sysdig TRT on our blog, or follow my bi-weekly security newsletter musings on LinkedIn.

Overview

On October 29, 2026, Ivanti updated its security advisory for Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) to include two additional vulnerabilities and released fixes for both. Ivanti rates CVE-2026-111357, a missing authentication for critical function vulnerability (CWE-306), with a CVSSv3.1 score of 8.8; it allows a local authenticated attacker to escalate privileges. CVE-2026-118527, classified as generation of predictable numbers or identifiers (CWE-340), has an Ivanti-assigned CVSSv3.0 score of 4.3 and, according to CISA's KEV entry, allows a remote authenticated attacker to upload attacker-controlled content to a known location on disk.

Per Ivanti, exploitation in the wild has already occurred prior to disclosure, affecting a limited number of customers when these flaws are chained with CVE-2026-104935, an authentication bypass by spoofing (CWE-290). Rapid7 covered the original disclosure on October 13, 2026, when a fix for CVE-2026-104935 was available but the privilege escalation component remained unpatched. Fixes are now available for all three vulnerabilities.

On October 30, 2026, CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527 were added to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) list of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEV), based on evidence of active exploitation.

The following scores and classifications are from Ivanti's updated advisory:

Note: The CVE record and Rapid7's vulnerability database rate CVE-2026-111357 at 7.0, using high attack complexity and unchanged scope. Ivanti assesses low attack complexity and changed scope, resulting in its score of 8.8. The table follows Ivanti's scores and classifications.

In its investigation, Volexity reports that UTA0576 used an exploit chain to gain unauthenticated root access to an appliance running 22.8R2.4, beginning on October 3, 2026. Its write-up identifies CVE-2026-104935 and CVE-2026-111357; Ivanti's updated advisory identifies CVE-2026-118527 as an additional component of the chain. Volexity observed credential theft and Active Directory queries for Windows LAPS passwords and BitLocker recovery keys.

The combined impact warrants emergency remediation despite the individual CVSS ratings. Ivanti Connect Secure is an enterprise VPN solution deployed at the network edge and has a history of zero-day exploitation, including in 2024 and 2025.

Mitigation guidance

Rapid7 recommends applying the available updates on an emergency basis outside of normal patching cycles. The October 13 fixes in 25.1.1.2 and 22.8R2.5 do not remediate CVE-2026-111357 or CVE-2026-118527.

Rapid7 also recommends investigating for compromise after patching. Volexity reports that the observed activity evades Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool, so a clean result does not rule out compromise. Preserve memory and logs before rebooting or resetting where feasible. If compromise is suspected, follow Ivanti's recovery steps and rotate potentially exposed credentials.

For current fixed versions and mitigation guidance, refer to Ivanti's security advisory. Its linked recovery procedure includes older release references.

Artifacts, evidence sources, and IOCs

The following guidance and artifacts are from Volexity's investigation:

Review requests to /dana-na/auth/url_default/welcome.cgi, especially URL/header mismatches involving X-DSCGI-PATH. Observed values include:

/home/runtime/dlogs/debuglog and /var/log/audit/audit.log: investigate evidence of selective deletion.

Volexity also provides YARA rules for request-header evidence and the privilege escalation payload in memory.

Rapid7 customers

Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose

Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527 with authenticated vulnerability checks available since the 2026-10-30 content release.
