4a158945977f.text:
The highest priorities for the transition to post-quantum cryptography are the basic building blocks of authenticated key-agreement protocols such as TLS. Without these building blocks in place, secure communication on the Internet will not be possible once cryptographically relevant quantum computers come online. However, today we rely on quantum-vulnerable cryptography for much more than TLS.

Privacy Pass is a protocol used by site operators like Cloudflare to help protect applications from abuse. One way we do this is by rate limiting individual clients so that no one client consumes too many of the site's resources. Normally this involves some combination of friction or loss of privacy for users: CAPTCHAs or other challenges to moderate traffic, along with accounts and fingerprinting to identify traffic.Privacy Pass was designed to avoid this tradeoff between friction and privacy. The basic idea is that a client gets issued a number of tokens, which they can redeem in exchange for access to the site. Crucially, each token is unlinkable to the client it was issued to, ensuring the client can use the site as they always had without sacrificing privacy.

With 10 years of deployment experience under our belts — using Privacy Pass for applications such as privacy proxies (like iCloud Private Relay) and relays (like Privacy Gateway) — we, along with others, are collaborating to bring the next generation of this technology to the web. One of our goals is to develop more sophisticated tools for managing agentic traffic that would otherwise consume too many resources and degrade performance for human visitors. Another goal is to foster a more open ecosystem by making it easier for more types of clients to participate. Achieving these goals requires developing new capabilities beyond what Privacy Pass offers today.

Given the trajectory, in this post we look at the prospects for post-quantum. In fact, we're in better shape than one might think. Privacy Pass still relies on classical cryptography, like RSA and elliptic curves. This means that a quantum attacker will be able to forge tokens at will and use them to bypass whatever security mechanism the site operator wants to implement (such as rate limiting). On the other hand, Privacy Pass is unconditionally private, meaning no attacker, quantum or not, can link the redemption of a token to its issuance. What's more, the new capabilities we're developing for this new generation of private authentication technology can and will be instantiated in a way that upholds the same guarantee: your interaction remains private even after Q-day.

This gives us a little breathing room, but we will need an alternative soon. This is an active area of research that has made significant strides in recent years. Still, just as is the case with other aspects of the transition, the primary challenge is the sheer size of post-quantum alternatives: ML-DSA-44 signatures are a whopping 2,420 bytes, while ECDSA-P256 signatures are just 64 bytes. And there's not much hope for drop-in replacements any time soon. Just as for TLS, we'll have to settle for primitives with higher cost and re-engineer our systems to bear this cost.

But what will those primitives be? In this post, we'll explore one potential future for post-quantum privacy on the web, made possible by a recent breakthrough in the design of blind signatures.

What we need to build: a brief look at MOLE

Let's start with an overview of this new technology, which is presently called MOLE ("Moderation Of unLinkable Endorsements"). We'll have much more to say about MOLE later on, but for now we'll highlight the details that are most relevant to cryptography.

One of the core components of Privacy Pass is a blind signature scheme, which allows a client to obtain a signature under an issuer's secret key without revealing to the issuer the message that it signed. The client can then reveal the message and blind signature later on without linking the signature to its issuance.

One type of Privacy Pass token consists of the message and blindly issued signature. To verify the token, the verifier needs the issuer's public key, and so necessarily learns the identity of the issuer. Thus while these tokens protect the identity of the client, they don't protect the identity of the issuer.

Of course, this is exactly what we want for some use cases. The identity of the issuer tells us something about what type of client is connecting to our edge, a signal we use to make decisions in some of our products and for some of our customers. For instance, a client might use a token issued by one of our customers to prove it is authorized to use the customer's VPN product.

However, for many use cases, this is more information than we actually need to make a decision to grant a client access to a resource. Normally we only care that the token was issued by some entity we trust. In fact, MOLE takes this a step further: the token should hide the identity of the issuer altogether so that we can't treat tokens differently based on who issued them. This guarantees equal treatment regardless of the type of client, making it easier for more clients to participate.

This issuer-hiding property is achieved through a new object called an endorsement. An endorsement is issued by an anchor and redeemed by a moderator. Before redemption, the client and moderator agree on an anchor set, the public keys of the anchors trusted by the moderator. During redemption, the client proves it was issued an endorsement by one of the anchors in the anchor set without revealing which one. Upon acceptance, the moderator issues the client the MOLE credential it will use to moderate the client's interaction with the site.

An endorsement can take many forms, but its key property is that it can be redeemed while hiding the identity of the anchor that issued it. There will also be many types of credentials, but because they're intended to be used by a particular moderator, they needn't be anchor-hiding or even publicly verifiable. This means that everything from blind signatures to anonymous credit tokens or anonymous rate-limited credentials can be used to instantiate MOLE credentials.

Now that we have a sense of what we're building, let's look at our options for post quantum.

A feast of cryptography

When designing cryptographic protocols, adaptability and efficiency are often in tension. Sometimes we know exactly what we want to build and can tailor a construction for that purpose; but the more we tailor the protocol for that use case, the harder it becomes to adapt that construction to a different use case.

Adaptability is essential for a system like MOLE. We're not just building one kind of credential system, but many. And the types of credentials we need are likely to change over time, especially on the web where we must constantly adapt to new traffic patterns and attacker behavior. To keep up, we need a set of building blocks that can be composed together into different protocols to meet different requirements.

Most of the post-quantum cryptographic schemes in wide use today come from larger families of constructions, but have been tuned for their particular application. ML-DSA is a good example here: the cryptographic framework from which this scheme was derived can be used to build a variety of things, but to make ML-DSA as compact as possible, its parameters have been carefully tailored to build an efficient and secure digital signature scheme. However, the same parameters would not necessarily be secure for other use cases.

We have come to view this as the central challenge for post-quantum anonymous credentials: to decouple parameter selection from protocol design. Classical credential systems take this for granted: for the most part, protocol designers don't need to think about the parameters of the elliptic curve they're using, allowing even non-experts in the design of elliptic curve cryptography to build useful things with it. Unfortunately, designing efficient post-quantum credentials still requires an enormous amount of expertise.

This situation seems to have changed, however. Earlier this year, we saw a breakthrough that represents a potential sea change for anonymous credentials.

VOLE-in-the-Head

The roots of this breakthrough go back several years. We'll pick up the story three years ago, with the VOLE-in-the-Head (VOLEitH) zero-knowledge proof system (Baum et al., Crypto 2023). A zero-knowledge proof system allows one to prove knowledge of a hidden witness, satisfying some public statement while keeping the witness private. For example, a zero-knowledge proof can be used to prove knowledge of an AES key K for which Y=AES(K,X), where X,Y are public. This proof can be transformed into a digital signature whose security reduces to the security of AES, with X,Y as the public key and K as the secret key. This is exactly the FAEST digital signature, a candidate in NIST's ongoing signature competition.

Compared to many contemporary proof systems, VOLEitH is relatively simple to understand and implement securely. VOLE stands for "Vector Oblivious Linear Evaluation" and is an interactive technique that gives two parties correlated random values. These correlations act like authentication tags, allowing the verifier to check that a computation on the hidden witness was performed correctly. In VOLEitH, the prover prepares locally what the two parties would normally generate together — hence “in the head” — then commits to those values and uses the Fiat-Shamir transformation (a widely used tool in cryptography) to select the parts the verifier checks. This step turns the interactive VOLE process into a non-interactive zero-knowledge proof.

Apart from its simplicity, VOLEitH is a fairly unremarkable proof system. It's not succinct in the way many other proof systems are: its proofs are asymptotically linear in the size of the witness and the arithmetic complexity of the statement being proved. However, VOLEitH is concretely very efficient for a particular type of statement, namely one that can be expressed as a set of equations over small binary fields.

One example is the relation Y=AES(K,X) we just discussed. We don't normally think of AES as a set of equations, but many of its computations are designed around arithmetic in GF(28), a field whose elements are single bytes. FAEST proofs for this statement are only about 4KB (NIST Round 3, 128s).

Another example is the KuMQuat signature scheme, in which the signer proves an instance of the Multivariate Quadratic (MQ) problem. Here we're given a system of random, quadratic equations of multiple variables over a small field, like GF(28). Mathematically, this MQ map P looks something like P(s) = (sTA1s + b1s,…,sTAms + bms) where s and each bi are length n vectors and each Ai is an n-by-n matrix. Given P,P(s) for random s, the MQ problem is to find s. We call it quadratic because we multiply the elements of s by itself.

The MQ problem is believed to be hard to solve even for a quantum computer. But because P is made up of quadratic equations, proving knowledge of a solution with VOLEitH is fairly cheap, yielding KuMQuat signatures as small as 2.6KB.

When compared to other post-quantum signatures like ML-DSA or FN-DSA, these numbers don't look especially impressive. But how VOLEitH compares to other schemes in a particular category of constructions is beside the point. For MOLE, we'll need to strike a balance between performance and the ability to build many types of credential systems. To that end, we need one more ingredient.

Multivariate signatures

Another way to build signatures from MQ maps involves embedding some additional mathematical structure into the map. In the Unbalanced Oil and Vinegar (UOV) signature scheme, the public key is an MQ map P, and a signature is a vector s satisfying P(s) = t, where t is obtained by hashing and salting the message to be signed.

The secret key for this signature scheme is a trapdoor for P with which the signer can derive solutions to the MQ equations. The trapdoor reveals to the signer a hidden partitioning of the variables of each quadratic equation into “oil” and “vinegar” variables. Oil variables are never multiplied by one another, so fixing the vinegar values turns the equations into a linear system that the signer can solve for the oil values. In the public key, oil and vinegar variables are mixed together in a way that hides this structure in the map.

UOV is also a candidate in NIST's ongoing signature standardization effort. It has one of the smallest signatures among the candidates, at just 135 bytes. The trade-off is that it has the largest public keys, at 46.6KB. MAYO is another multivariate candidate with much smaller public keys, at the cost of slightly larger signatures.

The key thing to take away here is that the arithmetic complexity of evaluating a UOV (or MAYO) signature is comparable to evaluating an MQ instance. Both are public quadratic maps over small binary fields, making them a good fit for VOLEitH. This brings us to the breakthrough.

Blind signatures from VOLE-in-the-Head and UOV

Earlier this year, a blind signature called PoMFRIT was published (Baum et al., USENIX Security 2026) that achieved what at the time was a record for candidate post-quantum constructions: 6.7KB for the blind signature itself and just a few hundred bytes for issuance. PoMFRIT is based on VOLE-in-the-Head and the MAYO multivariate signature. We can easily drive the size of the signature down to 4.3KB by swapping MAYO out for UOV. (This figure uses NIST round 3 parameters for UOV (uov-Ip) and FAEST-EM-128s.) The trade-off is larger public keys, but this pays off in applications where a public key can be cached and used sufficiently often.

This is competitive with state-of-the-art lattice-based constructions. But the really good news is that building blocks of PoMFRIT can easily be reconfigured into all of the credential systems we've considered for MOLE, including endorsements. More on this in a bit: for now, let's look at how PoMFRIT works in more detail.

A well-known paradigm for designing blind signatures is the following. First, the client places the message in the cryptographic equivalent of a sealed envelope, called a commitment. For our purposes, a commitment is simply the hash of the message together with some randomness generated by the client. To complete issuance, the signer simply signs the commitment directly.

To construct the blind signature, the client produces a zero-knowledge proof of knowledge of the signature and the randomness it used to compute the commitment, called the opening. A verifier would use the signer's public key to verify this proof.

Let's define a bit of notation to make this clearer:

The client generates an opening r and sends a commitment c=H(m,r) to its message m to the issuer.

The issuer produces a signature s=Sign(sk,c) and sends it to the client. It doesn’t learn the message as it’s hidden behind the hash.

Finally, the client produces a proof π of knowledge of s,r for which Verify(pk,H(m,r))=1,

The proof π is the blind signature. It can be verified by any party in possession of the issuer's public key pk and the message m.

Unlinkability comes from the client presenting entirely different objects during the two phases: a commitment is shown to the issuer during issuance, and a zero-knowledge proof is shown to a verifier during presentation. Even if the issuer and verifier collude or are the same entity, they cannot link the sessions.

The size of the proof π is dominated by evaluation of the hash, so we need to choose a hash function that is friendly for our proof system. For most proof systems, such proof-friendly hashes are not well studied, but for VOLEitH it turns out that the Keccak permutation used in SHAKE and TurboSHAKE is a good choice. Keccak’s bitwise operations translate natively into VOLEitH constraints: XOR becomes addition, AND becomes multiplication, and rotations simply rearrange values. (Many popular SNARKs, by contrast, are designed for large prime fields, making byte- and bit-oriented operations less natural to express.)

Nevertheless, Keccak evaluations end up being the largest component of the VOLEitH proof, so we need to make sure we're using only the minimum necessary number of permutations. PoMFRIT requires two: one for the commitment and another for the signature. Concretely, the statement we prove is roughly P(s)=H(H(m,r),rs) where s is the signature, rs is a salt chosen by the issuer, P is the issuer's UOV public key, and H denotes the Keccak permutation with the output truncated to the appropriate length, which also prevents anyone from inverting.

From blind signatures to endorsements and beyond

Recall that for MOLE endorsements, we need something like a blind signature, but one that doesn't reveal the anchor that issued it. That is, we now have a sequence of anchor keys P1,…,PN, and the statement we now want to prove is Pi(s)=H(H(m,r),rs) for some anchor key Pi whose index i is now part of the hidden witness.

With some care, we can write this as a set of constraints with roughly the same cost: two hashes and one MQ evaluation. We need to prove a bit more about the witness. What exactly? We won't spoil it for you: ZK circuit design is part of the craft of cryptographic engineering that makes it so fun. We'll just say the kind of thinking needed here is transferable to just about any modern proof system you might encounter.

Even more advanced credential systems can be constructed in this framework, including the aforementioned anonymous credit tokens and anonymous rate-limited credentials. In both of these cases, the primary cost is an additional hash or two. Each of these also requires proving that part of the witness (e.g., the credit count) is in some expected range, but this is low cost in VOLEitH.

Indeed, for every construction we have considered so far for MOLE, the primary cost is the size of the Keccak evaluation and how many times we need to evaluate it. This means that finding ways to reduce the amount of hashing yields improvements across the board.

Optimizations

Before we go any further, we need to acknowledge that cryptanalysis of multivariate cryptography is still relatively immature. We have seen advances against several parameter regimes in just the last couple of years, Both UOV and MAYO have weathered these attacks well, and an outright break of UOV and even MAYO seems more unlikely with every passing year. But we should at least expect the parameters to change in a way that adds a bit of cost to our constructions.

On the other hand, it's not uncommon for credential systems used in practice to adopt a less-than-conservative security posture for the sake of performance in so far as it affects forgery resistance. This typically means relying on stronger-than-usual computational assumptions. That is, it's possible that a (pre-quantum) attack might come along that breaks anonymous credit tokens, but not ECDSA, despite the fact that they both use the same elliptic curve.

Using fewer hashes

PoMFRIT achieved its size record by doing precisely the same thing. Recall that the blind signature requires proving two hash evaluations, one by the client and the other by the issuer. PoMFRIT observes that VOLEitH proof generation can be split into two stages. In the first stage, the client commits to a random mask. It then hashes the message normally (outside of the ZK circuit), combines the result with the mask, and sends the masked target to the issuer. The issuer uses the UOV trapdoor to find a preimage of this target. In the second stage, the client completes the proof that the preimage and previously committed mask are consistent. The hash remains part of the protocol, but the issuer — acting as the VOLEitH verifier — can compute it directly rather than requiring the zero-knowledge proof to reproduce it.

This strategy substantially reduces proof size, but it also changes our security posture. The plain UOV assumption is that no (quantum) attacker can find a pre-image for a random target without knowledge of the trapdoor. The corresponding one-more-UOV assumption (analogous to the one-more-MAYO assumption in the PoMFRIT paper) neatly captures the additional information available to the attacker as a result of this kind of optimization. The assumption, then, is that this additional information doesn't lead to an attack.

This assumption may turn out to be overly optimistic. Recently, researchers at the University of California, San Diego, and INRIA managed to forge a 1024-bit RSA signature using a Privacy Pass issuer as a signing oracle. Fortunately, Privacy Pass uses 2048-bit RSA, which, in concert with other defense mechanisms, provides a pretty good security margin. Likewise, for UOV we might consider using NIST Level 3 parameters instead of Level 1.

In any case, a bit more study will be required before we rely too heavily on these kinds of optimizations. It's worth emphasizing that a break here would only impact an attacker's ability to forge tokens, not the attacker's ability to violate a client's privacy.

Making each hash cheaper

Standard SHAKE uses a 1600-bit Keccak state with 24 applications of an underlying round function. However, since the SHA-3 standard was published, many have come to believe that 24 rounds is just too much crypto. TurboSHAKE works the same way, except the permutation uses 12 rounds instead of 24. This substantially reduces the size of VOLEitH proofs. In fact, we're quite comfortable with this security margin, and not just for this application.

Another change to Keccak that reduces the proof size is to reduce the size of the state. 256 bits of the state are reserved for the capacity to get 128 bits security. That leaves 1344 bits that can be hashed in one go, which is more than we need. Reducing the state by half to 800 bits leaves us with a rate of 544 bits, which is plenty. On top of that, it even increases the security at the same number of rounds, as an attacker has less to play with. The smaller state means we’re using half the multiplications in our circuit, which reduces the size of the proof.

Leaning into multivariate

In an ideal world, we could avoid proving conventional hashes altogether by replacing each hash with something that composes more natively with the algebraic structure of our primitives. Indeed, those familiar with Pedersen commitments and their use in elliptic curve cryptography may wonder if commitments can be constructed from multivariate cryptography.

This might look something like this: Fix public, random MQ maps F and G and commit to a message m using c=(m+F(r),G(r)). The advantage of this approach is that the degree of the constraints is the same as the degree of the constraints for the UOV signature. Not only does this make the proof smaller, it makes it far simpler, since we avoid evaluating symmetric crypto in ZK altogether.

We experimented with this approach for our application, and it yielded some impressive results. However, it's not at all clear yet if the parameter regime in which multivariate commitments yield an improvement is also secure. Notably, the risk here is not just to unforgeability, but also to client privacy. A lot more study is needed.

Another direction is to build an MQ-friendly pseudorandom generator (PRG).

For typical VOLEitH parameters, adding an extra witness bit adds ten bits to the proof. There is a neat trick to make this a lot cheaper: only one bit of proof per bit of witness! Instead of using VOLEitH directly, we commit to a (relatively) short key. That key we stretch into a larger bitstream using a PRG with low-degree so that it can be computed cheaply in the circuit. Now, to add a witness bit w, we get one extra bit k from the PRG, and store the bit w XOR k in the proof.

There is a performance trade-off: we need to compute the PRG and the witnesses start at degree 2 instead of 1. That especially increases prover time. Also the benefits on proof size only start to pay off when you need a decent number of witness bits.

And of course you need a PRG! You can create a PRG using a random MQ instance, but that’s very slow and seems overly conservative. At the other end is the Goldreich PRG, which can be seen as an as-sparse-as-possible MQ PRG. We’d want something in between, but such PRGs haven’t received much study.

Is MOLE ready for post-quantum?

We already have post-quantum privacy today, so we have some time before we need to have a solution in place, but now is the time to develop alternatives.

Multivariate cryptography looks to be a promising basis for easily building a variety of anonymous tokens and credentials. We're currently developing two schemes in this framework: VOLE-IHAT, a candidate for MOLE endorsements, and VOLE-ACT, a candidate for MOLE credentials. Our current cost estimates for these are shown in the table below. The numbers here are subject to change as we analyze and develop these constructions. We use UOV (uov-Ip) in each case, which means the public keys are all 46.6KB. VOLEitH uses the same parameters as FAEST-EM-128s:

issuance

presentation

PoMFRIT (with UOV)

<1KB

4.3KB (redemption)

VOLE-IHAT

5.6KB

6.5KB (redemption)

VOLE-ACT

5.4KB

12.0KB (spend)

These numbers are significantly larger than their classical counterparts. This comes as no great surprise, as "PQ is big" is really the main hallmark of the transition across the board. However, replacing RSA blind signatures with PoMFRIT has comparable overhead to replacing ECDSA with ML-DSA. The runtimes of these protocols are also excellent: each operation takes just a few milliseconds with our implementation. (Runtime can be improved by quite a bit, though at the cost of higher communication.)

If these numbers hold, then we've already reached an important milestone: the transition to PQ anonymous credentials for the web can now shift from cryptography design to protocol engineering. In other words, we think we can make these numbers work. For example, whereas classical blind signatures might be cheap enough to redeem on every request, we'll have to figure out how to amortize a single redemption over multiple requests.

We have some work to do before we get there. First, we need to make sure our protocols are sound, in particular by producing security proofs for them that show they are secure as long as UOV is secure. Second, we need to wait a bit for cryptanalysis of UOV to catch up. We encourage cryptographers to spend time with multivariate cryptography. Once the parameters stabilize, we believe these schemes will find a place in a ton of useful applications. We've only just scratched the surface so far.

0df7f77739ef.text:
The recent refrigerator hacks wreaking havoc across European supermarkets is a lesson in how shared weaknesses in operational technology (OT) can spread across a whole supply chain.

On the night of Oct. 11, an unknown attacker reportedly compromised refrigeration controls used by hundreds of French supermarkets, triggering extended defrost cycles in refrigerators and freezers across the country. The incident caused millions of euros in damage across roughly 700 affected stores in France alone, spoiling food, damaging equipment, and even reportedly starting some fires in the process.

The technology leveraged in these attacks included Danfoss refrigeration controllers, as well as Dixell and Copeland XWEB systems. It's unclear how the threat actor gained access to these systems.

However, the Danfoss controllers at the center of this campaign ran Internet-accessible Web servers. Many were accessible using default login credentials: "admin" as the username and the current date as the password. CERT-FR made a number of recommendations in an advisory to affected supermarkets, such as changing default passwords, factory resetting compromised equipment, and updating firmware. Though to that last point, Danfoss told AFP that many of the attacks involved legacy products that no longer receive updates.

Related:Les supermarchés de l'UE paient d'un firmware de réfrigérateur non mis à jour

Shared Infrastructure, Big Consequences

What stands out about the French supermarket attacks is how a shared weakness in refrigeration infrastructure appears to have enabled disruption across hundreds of stores. While investigators have not publicly confirmed the initial access vector, the incident raises questions about the risks created when organizations rely on similar technologies, deployment models, and remote-access practices.

Chris St. Myers, director of SentinelLABS, says evidence suggests a common exposure problem, rather than market concentration, may have facilitated this issue.

"CERT-FR confirmed that the French compromises involved Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers, along with Copeland and Dixell XWEB systems. These technologies are deployed across many retail environments, often with similar remote access requirements and configurations," St. Meyers says. "That creates opportunities for attackers to reuse the same techniques across otherwise unrelated organizations."

Thomas Plank, CEO of industrial security firm Tributech, similarly diagnosed common exposure as a core issue behind the attacks.

"What's concentrated is the setup. Across chains and countries, it's the same model: remote-management controllers reachable from the internet, often on out-of-support firmware, maintained by a small number of contractors who look after hundreds of stores from one place," Plank tells Dark Reading. "When everyone runs the same risky pattern through the same few channels, one way in reaches many retailers at once, across borders, overnight. That's why this looks like a campaign rather than a string of unlucky stores."

Related:EU Grocers Pay a Steep Price for Unpatched Fridge Firmware

Fridge Attacks Offer Familiar Lessons

It's highly unusual and hardly precedented for a cyberattack to have such a significant impact on the food supply chain, but it's not the only incident like it in recent memory.

A similar attack hit refrigeration and freezer systems in stores across other countries at the beginning of November, including Belgium, Estonia, Germany, Ireland, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Spain, and Sweden. Around the same time, attackers targeted the refrigeration of three blood banks operated by the national French Blood Establishment, though the attack was stopped before blood plasma was damaged.

For as alarming and impactful these incidents may seem, supply chain targeting has become more common in recent years with 2021's Colonial Pipeline attack, Iran's recent targeting of fuel monitoring systems around the US, and 2024's Change Healthcare incident.

Related:Taiwan Bullet Train Hack Highlights Cybersecurity Gaps in Rail Systems

The danger is clear, especially in the context of a supermarket. Piotr Buliński, chief technology officer (CTO) of Internet of Things (IoT) device management firm Qbee, says a supermarket chain runs thousands of small, unattended OT systems between refrigeration, HVAC, and building management. "Each one is 'just a few controllers,' so nobody treats them as critical infrastructure," he says. "Yet when they fail, the damage is immediate and physical."

The Perils of Securing OT

These incidents remind us once again about the importance of securing critical infrastructure.

Updating OT systems is a challenging task in their own right because of the downtime often required. Much of the critical technology holding up industrial processes is intended to operate for years (if not decades) on end, while the organizations relying on OT can often include those too under-resourced to have dedicated security staff, like municipalities, or indeed, supermarkets.

Even as these problems have gotten a little easier to address over the years and many dedicated firms have risen to address these challenges, organizations still struggle to secure OT.

St. Meyers believes retail OT has historically received less security attention than traditional industrial environments, despite carrying many of the same underlying risks. He says this is possibly in part because refrigeration, HVAC, and building management systems are "often deployed and maintained outside the traditional IT security organization," despite being OT.

Plank agrees. He says one solution for retailers is to verify commands at the device level against engineering limits, as "no freezer should ever accept a command to go to 50°C, whoever sends it and whatever channel it arrives on," referencing the extreme temperatures some targeted equipment reached during the attacks.

For organizations outside the sphere of influence that want to learn from what happened here, there are several lessons: Don't use default passwords, take inventory of where and how industrial technologies are internet accessible, remove internet exposure wherever possible, and make sure all points of access are secured.

Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat research at Sophos, tells Dark Reading that generally, this incident should be seen as a warning to retailers. "Industrial systems, from energy production to water management to food refrigeration, must be secured," he says, "and at a minimum not accessible to malicious hackers via the Internet."

Buckle up Metasploit-Framework enthusiasts because we have another action packed release for you. I'm talking, unauthenticated remote code execution modules in some of the biggest names in network perimeter devices like Citrix NetScaler and Cisco Secure Email Gateway. That's not all, we have an authenticated GitLab CI/CD regular expression integer overflow RCE module that was recently making head lines among many other awesome exploit modules. Looking for auxiliary modules? We've got you covered this release with a Flowise authentication bypass and a OpenBullet2 NTLMv2 hash disclosure, because who doesn't love collecting and cracking (or in some cases relaying) NTLM hashes am I right or am I right? In our continued effort to expand the payloads supported by the framework this week we saw fetch payload support for LoongArch. Lastly, if you're ever on an engagement or at home doing some testing and you see something that's not supported in Metasploit-Framework that you'd like to see supported, either drop us suggested-features issue on GitHub or trying throwing up a Pull Request, we'd love to hear from you. 75fbaed719ea.text:
Rogue AI agents hit Hugging Face, a U.S. Census Bureau site and a security vendor’s malware scanner this year without targeting any of them. Third-party risk programs have no line for that.

Between July and October, AI agents working on evaluation and research tasks for OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta broke into real organizations that nobody had chosen as targets. Hugging Face and a U.S. Census Bureau site were among them, along with dozens of others. Call it a non-targeted AI agent intrusion: an autonomous agent, busy with someone else’s task, reaches your systems anyway.

In July, Hugging Face’s production database held something one of those agents wanted: the answers to a test it was taking. Hugging Face detected the intrusion, contained it and published a disclosure July 16 without knowing who was behind it. Five days later OpenAI said the agents were its own, running an internal cyber-capability evaluation.

Security leaders should look closely at that order of events. Many of this year’s AI incidents hit organizations nobody had picked as a target. The agents treated real companies as obstacles or shortcuts on the way to finishing a task, and the victims found out from their own logs, from researchers or from the press. Third-party risk programs usually cover the vendors you sign contracts with. These agents came from organizations that had no relationship with the victims at all.

Which organizations did rogue AI agents hit this year?

AI security firm Pillar Security, which keeps a running list, counted 21 public disclosures between July and mid-October in which agents from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta acted outside their authorized scope. The cases that reached outside organizations look like this:

Disclosed

Whose agent

Who got hit

What the agent did

Oct. 1

OpenAI, as identified by Asymmetric Security

About 50 organizations, including U.S. agencies, the International Energy Agency and Mayo Clinic

Probed sites through remote browsers and proxies, using private scanner accounts and a self-expiring inbox

Sept. 24–30

Unknown

Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD)

Chained two zero-days in the Zammad helpdesk to reach root, then moved to other services and took data

Sept. 25

OpenAI

A U.S. Census Bureau site, one of more than 100 organizations OpenAI said it notified

Logged in with credentials found online

Sept. 18

Google

Three unnamed companies (incidents in May)

Guessed a password at one company and used credentials from a public repository at the other two, then stopped

Aug. 5

Meta

An unnamed third-party service, during third-party testing

Exploited a vulnerability after a testing misconfiguration gave the model internet access; reportedly altered part of the affected company’s internal environment

July 30

Anthropic

Three organizations, including a security company

Published a malicious PyPI package that ran on 15 systems, including the security company’s malware scanner; the package stole that company’s credentials, and the agent used them to reach more of its infrastructure

July 16–21

OpenAI

Hugging Face

Escaped its evaluation and ran code on 41 production workers, then took credentials and reached internal clusters

The Hugging Face case is the best documented. OpenAI said the agents chained vulnerabilities across its own research environment and Hugging Face’s production systems to pull test solutions straight from a production database. Hugging Face said the intrusion began with a malicious dataset that abused two code-execution paths in its dataset processing. Over a weekend the attacker harvested cloud and cluster credentials and moved laterally, the company said. Its analysis covered more than 17,000 recorded attacker actions.

The DIVD breach is the one without an owner. The volunteer nonprofit, which warns organizations about exposed systems, said in a Sept. 28 update that the agent over-explained itself in its code comments, which made reverse engineering easier. Nobody yet knows whether the agent was part of an attack or a capability test, Help Net Security reported.

How do rogue AI agents reach companies they aren’t targeting?

Read the incidents together and four patterns stand out.

Shared test infrastructure fails in shared ways. Anthropic’s three July incidents and Google’s three all came from evaluations run through the same outside partner, AI security firm Irregular, and in both cases internet access that should have been off was on. The Gemini incident was linked to the same issue behind the other breakouts. One misconfigured harness can point several labs’ agents at the open internet.

Names collide. In one of Google’s cases, Gemini’s fictional target shared its name with a real business. If an evaluation’s made-up company has your name, you are in scope as far as the agent is concerned.

Your data can be the answer key. Hugging Face held benchmark solutions. DIVD held vulnerability reports that weren’t public yet. Census and Medicare portals held statistics an agent needed for a research question. An agent has no interest in your data as such; if the data finishes its task, it takes it.

Leaked secrets get used, even by agents that aren’t attacking you. Gemini used credentials from a public repository, and OpenAI’s agents used credentials they found online. Between Sept. 28 and Oct. 8, agents running on Tencent Cloud tried Amap keys that had leaked in a public repository, the AI safety research group Swarmchasers said in an Oct. 14 report. Tencent said later that the agents were evaluating third-party models. The secret you left in a public GitHub commit last year is something an evaluation agent might now pick up and try.

Also Read:

Why don’t third-party risk programs catch rogue AI agents?

Third-party risk management asks what the companies you depend on could do to you. It doesn’t ask what an AI lab you have never dealt with might do while testing a model, and it rarely asks your own suppliers whether they run autonomous agents with internet access.

Detection is the other gap. Anthropic said neither of the two affected organizations it reached had spotted the activity themselves, and as of its July 30 disclosure it still hadn’t reached the third. Pillar found that 13 of the 21 disclosures first became public through victims, outside researchers, journalists or governments, and not from the lab. Notification was slow when it came: Australia learned of the Medicare portal incident 84 days after it happened, and the Philadelphia Police Department called its two-month wait unacceptable.

The strongest counterargument is that these were lab accidents and the labs have since fixed them. Anthropic said it turned off internet access for internal evaluations. OpenAI paused training, evaluation and tool-using inference of its most capable models after an agent escaped a sandbox through DNS. Those steps cover a handful of companies. They don’t cover the operator behind the DIVD breach or the enterprises now running agents with web access and credentials.

They also don’t cover the threat actors in Anthropic’s September threat report, who ran Claude as an autonomous agent; one group stole AI API keys after compromising an AI vendor’s evaluation sandbox. Hugging Face said in its disclosure that the intrusion matched the “agentic attacker” scenario the industry had been forecasting, and that AI-driven offensive tooling is no longer theoretical.

Reps. Josh Gottheimer (D-N.J.) and Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) announced the Stop Rogue AI Act (H.R. 10362) on Sept. 9. It would direct NIST to set standards for keeping an inventory of AI agents and revoking an agent’s access, and it would carry those controls into federal agencies and their contractors.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office served OpenAI with an investigative subpoena on Sept. 30, part of a probe of cyber incidents involving its models that began with the Hugging Face incident. On Oct. 13, more than 400 scientists, including Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, signed an open letter asking for an international body to track containment failures and for organizations to report those incidents to it, and eventually to the public.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency followed on Nov. 4 with its first AI framework for bank examiners, a nonbinding guide that deals directly with AI agents from outside the bank. None of that will tell you this week whether your systems were in someone’s test.

What should CISOs do about rogue AI agents now?

Add five things to the program you already run.

Ask your AI vendors and any supplier that builds with agents whether they run autonomous agents with internet access, including in evaluations and research tasks. Ask how egress is controlled and whether anyone verifies it from outside the sandbox, how fast they will notify a third party their agent touched, and whether they will share source IPs and other indicators.

Hunt for agent traffic. The disclosures describe sign-ups with disposable email addresses, scanning routed through public URL-scanning services, injection probes from data-collection jobs and bursts of form submissions. Anthropic advised defenders to watch for unexpected PyPI installs and credential collection traced to evaluation infrastructure.

Clean up what agents harvest. Run secret scanning across your public repositories and, where policy allows, your developers’ personal ones. Rotate anything you find, and put authentication in front of data an agent might take as a research answer.

Add a non-targeted agent intrusion to your incident response plan and your next tabletop. Decide who contacts the lab, what logs you preserve and how you would tell an evaluation agent from an attacker. Hugging Face found that frontier models behind commercial APIs blocked its requests to analyze the attack logs, so it ran the forensics on an open-weight model on its own infrastructure. Have that option vetted before you need it.

Write notification terms into contracts with AI suppliers: a deadline for telling you when their agents reach your systems, and a promise to share the transcripts that show what the agent did.

Questions for AI vendors and suppliers that build with agents

Question

A good answer includes

Red flag

Do you run autonomous agents with internet access, including in evaluations and research tasks?

A yes or no, with the environments named

"Only in testing" with no detail on what testing can reach

How is egress from those agents controlled?

Network-level blocks, not instructions to the model

Egress "disabled by default" with no check that it stayed off

Is egress verified from outside the sandbox?

An external test or monitor that would see traffic leaving

Verification only from inside the agent's own environment

Do you use a third-party evaluation provider? Which one?

The provider's name and how its harness is isolated

No answer, or "we can't say"

What credentials do your agents hold, and for how long?

Per-run, short-lived, scoped credentials

Shared or long-lived keys reused across runs

Can you revoke an agent's access mid-task?

A named owner and a tested kill path

No owner, or never tested

How fast will you notify a third party your agent touched?

A deadline in hours, in writing

"As soon as practicable"

What will you share when you notify?

Source IPs, timestamps, other indicators and the agent's transcripts

A summary only

Sample notification clause

Starting language for counsel to adapt. It is not legal advice. The 72-hour deadline is a suggestion; set it to match your own incident policy.

AI agent activity. Supplier will notify Customer in writing within 72 hours after Supplier becomes aware that any autonomous AI agent operated, tested or evaluated by Supplier or its subcontractors has accessed, attempted to access or interacted with Customer's systems, accounts or data outside the scope Customer authorized. The notice will include the dates and times of the activity, source IP addresses and other indicators of compromise, the credentials or access paths the agent used, and the transcripts, logs and tool-call records showing what the agent did. Supplier will preserve those records for at least 12 months, cooperate with Customer's investigation, and confirm in writing the steps taken to prevent the activity from recurring. Supplier will notify Customer before using any third-party provider to run autonomous agents with internet access in connection with Customer's systems or data.

Your side of the fence

Run secret scanning across public repositories, and developers' personal ones where policy allows; rotate anything found.

Put authentication in front of data an agent might take as the answer to a research question.

Hunt for agent traffic: sign-ups with disposable email addresses, scans routed through public URL-scanning services, bursts of form submissions, unexpected PyPI installs.

Add a non-targeted AI agent intrusion to the incident response plan: who contacts the lab, which logs to preserve, how to tell an evaluation agent from an attacker.

Vet a self-hosted, open-weight model for forensics. Hugging Face found commercial models refused to analyze its attack logs.

Run the scenario in your next tabletop.

Takeaways

Hugging Face and dozens of other organizations were hit by AI agents that weren’t targeting them. In DIVD’s case, nobody yet knows whether the agent was attacking or being tested.

Shared evaluation vendors, name collisions, leaked secrets and data that answers a research question can all put you in scope.

Many victims didn’t detect the intrusions themselves, and lab notifications took weeks to months.

Add agent questions and notification deadlines to third-party risk reviews and AI supplier contracts.

Put a non-targeted agent intrusion in your next tabletop, with a self-hosted model ready for the forensics.

References

Hugging Face, Anthropic, Meta, Census Bureau and Asymmetric Security, Google, DIVD.

The US government is urging healthcare, chemical, food, and transportation organizations to harden their industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems.

Over the past weeks, threat actors have been hacking monitoring systems to tamper with fridges and freezers in supermarkets and blood banks across Europe, causing millions in losses.

Hundreds of supermarkets were hit on October 11, when the attackers turned the temperatures in fridges to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) and set freezers to defrost, spoiling food and, in some cases, causing fires.

A second wave of attacks hit more than 100 supermarkets and a blood bank this week, but only supermarkets suffered losses. Quick action from staff prevented the compromise of blood products and samples, the French Blood Establishment (EFS) said.

Russian hacktivist groups such as Noname057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance reportedly claimed hacking Danfoss, leading to speculation that they mounted the supermarket attacks. However, nothing has been confirmed, and Iranian hacktivists or state-sponsored hackers may also be responsible, BBC notes.

CISA, the FBI, HHS, USDA, and DoT say they “are aware of malicious cyber actors targeting electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities.”

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

“The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards,” the agencies note (PDF).

Hackers may exploit authentication bypasses, code injection, and weak configurations to access the management systems and tamper with refrigerator and cold storage systems’ temperature or cause denial-of-view conditions, the agencies say.

According to internet intelligence firm Censys, out of 6,695 internet-exposed refrigeration controllers identified on October 9, only 3,124 (or 47%) remain accessible from the web as of November 5.

The company’s analysis covers the widely used Copeland/Dixell XWEB and Danfoss StoreView controllers: XWEB exposure dropped 35% (3,708 to 2,420), while StoreView dropped 76% (3,004 to 708).

Per the US government’s recommendations, taking the control systems off the internet is the best action organizations can take to prevent attacks. If web access is necessary, these systems should be protected by a firewall or edge device.

Organizations should also isolate OT devices, restrict access to trusted identities, enforce strong password policies and phishing-resistant multifactor authentication, keep systems updated, maintain backups offsite, and enable logging and monitoring.

09c2aac1da3e.text:
Critical Kubernetes CVEs arrive constantly. Some hit an operator or controller, some the Linux kernel underneath your nodes, others the container images your teams ship every day. Each one comes with a CVSS score and an urgent recommendation to patch.

What it doesn’t come with is context. A CVSS score tells you how bad a flaw could be in theory. It can’t tell you whether the vulnerable component runs in your clusters, whether anyone could actually exploit it, or what it can reach. Without those answers, teams either scramble to patch everything at once or let the CVE sit in a backlog until it’s forgotten.

Kubernetes makes this harder than most environments. Workloads are ephemeral, permissions are spread across roles, bindings and service accounts, and a single foothold can travel from a pod to a node, from a node to the cloud account, or through a privileged operator to everything it manages.

This post walks through a repeatable approach for triaging any Kubernetes CVE in Orca, then puts it to work on a real example: Copy Fail, a Linux kernel flaw affecting nodes across nearly every major cloud and operating system.

How to triage a Kubernetes CVE: Four questions to ask

Whatever the CVE, effective triage comes down to the same four questions. Orca answers each one from a single platform for cloud security, across every cluster and the cloud accounts they run in.

Where does it run?

Is it internet exposed?

Is it exploitable?

What can it reach?

Each answer narrows the list for the next, so a CVE that touches dozens of clusters ends with a short, ranked set of actions. Here’s how that looks on a real example.

The example: Copy Fail (CVE-2026-31431)

Copy Fail is a bug in the Linux kernel that lets an ordinary user quietly give themselves full admin (root) access. In Kubernetes, that means an attacker who gets into any container can take over the node it runs on, and from there, potentially everything that node can reach. Here’s how Orca takes you from the headline to a fix.

Step 1: Find which nodes and images are affected

Orca’s emerging threats feed, From the News, flags Copy Fail with a plain-language summary and recommended fix. From there, search CVE-2026-31431 in the Vulnerabilities view, part of Orca’s agentless vulnerability management, to see every affected node, node pool and image across clusters and clouds, with the fixed kernel version for each.

Prefer plain English? Ask Orca AI, an AI reasoning engine for security teams, “Which Kubernetes nodes are affected by CVE-2026-31431?” and get the same answer in seconds.

Step 2: Check whether affected nodes or pods are internet exposed

Copy Fail needs a foothold inside a pod first, so checking the node alone isn’t enough. A node can sit on a private network and still run a pod that’s reachable from the internet through a LoadBalancer or an Ingress. If that pod is compromised, the attacker lands on the node’s kernel just the same. Click into an affected node to see its asset details, including whether the node or any workload running on it is publicly accessible, and how many high-severity risks it carries. Nodes with any internet-facing path go to the top of the list. Nodes with no exposure still get patched, just on a normal cycle.

Step 3: Confirm whether the CVE is exploitable

Open the Copy Fail risk on that node to see the vulnerable kernel package it affects, along with Orca’s exploitability and risk scoring details. Copy Fail has public exploit code, so the answer is yes, and on a node with an internet-exposed workload, that moves it from “patch soon” to “patch now.”

Step 4: Map the attack path from node to cloud

A node escape is only as dangerous as what the node can access. Use attack path analysis to see how an attacker could move to the cloud roles, secrets or crown jewel data within reach, all in one ranked path. That’s the alert you patch first.

Go further with Orca: Remediate, prevent, and prove progress

That’s the triage done. But finding the risk is only part of the job, and Orca helps with the rest too.

Prove progress to leadership. When leadership asks where things stand, you shouldn’t need to scramble and pull a spreadsheet together to answer. The K8s & Container Security dashboard shows how many clusters and nodes are still affected, and that number drops as patches roll out, so one view shows both your current risk and your progress.

Patch without letting new risk in. Teams keep deploying while patches roll out, and every new pod is a possible foothold. Orca’s Admission Controller checks each workload before it’s admitted, stopping new privileged or host-namespace pods, which make it easier to take over a node from a compromised container, from landing in affected clusters. Policies can warn or block depending on what you need, and every decision is logged in Orca alongside the CVE you’re tracking.

Stay audit-ready. An unpatched critical vulnerability is an audit finding waiting to happen. Orca automatically maps it to the regulatory compliance frameworks you report on, such as PCI DSS 4.0 and SOC 2, so you know which controls are affected now and have the evidence ready once remediation is done, instead of scrambling for it later.

Cut the time to fix. Orca opens tickets in tools you already use with the affected nodes and fixed kernel version already filled in, so engineers start fixing instead of investigating, and you can track every ticket through to closure. Where patching has to wait, disabling the affected kernel module is a quick interim mitigation.

Catch an attack before the patch lands. Rolling new images across a fleet takes time, and that window is when attackers move. Orca’s cloud detection and response monitors affected workloads for suspicious activity, so if someone tries to use the foothold, you know right away and can respond.

Together, that’s the difference between knowing about a CVE and being done with it.

A repeatable workflow for the next Kubernetes CVE

Kubernetes CVEs aren’t slowing down, and patching everything the moment it’s disclosed isn’t realistic. The teams that stay ahead are the ones that know where those CVEs are throughout their environment, and which ones need to get remediated first.

Orca helps you do exactly that. From the first alert to the closed ticket, the Orca Cloud Security Platform shows you where a CVE runs, whether it’s exposed, whether it’s exploitable, what it can reach, and how it affects your compliance posture. Copy Fail is one example. The same workflow works for whatever CVE lands next.

See it in your own environment. Request a demo and we’ll walk through how Orca triages the Kubernetes CVEs that matter most to your clusters. To go deeper on Orca’s Kubernetes and Container Security capabilities, download the data sheet.

b0e8c4251f79.text:
The use of a new AI-powered offensive security tool by cyber threat actors appears to be spreading well beyond the campaigns first identified.

This tool, called ARTEX, is an open-source, AI model-driven, autonomous penetration testing framework released on GitHub by a user known as ‘Autumn-27’ in July 2026.

While ARTEX has already been integrated in several known malicious campaigns since October, a new report by internet traffic scan provider Censys estimated its use could be much more widespread than previously thought.

ARTEX's Growing Use by Cyber Threat Actors

Written in Go with an embedded Next.js web console, ARTEX offers an offensive command-and-control (C2) platform that communicates with several AI agents and can be plugged in to large language models (LLMs).

In October, two threat intelligence companies attributed its use as part of threat actor operations.

First, in early October, CrowdStrike linked ARTEX to a campaign against South Korean financial institutions. The analysts found ARTEX was used alongside Anthropic’s Claude AI model during the campaign, which ran from late September to early October 2026. CrowdStrike assessed with moderate confidence that the attacker is a Chinese speaker and financially motivated.

Later in October, Microsoft linked ARTEX to a large-scale compromise of ConnectWise customer tenants which led to IT management software provider taking a number of its cloud services offline. Microsoft attributed the campaign to Storm-0940, a China-state-aligned cyber threat actor also known as CovertNetwork-1658 or ORB07.

More recently, on November 4, the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) warned financial and cryptocurrency organizations that a threat group tracked as ‘Crafty Falcon’ had been targeting them in successive attacks using several AI-powered tools, including ARTEX.

The original GitHub repository for ARTEX was taken down by its creator in October 2026 due to widespread threat actor abuse. The author claimed they were not involved in the ARTEX-linked attacks and that the tool was only meant for authorized penetration testing.

Nevertheless, the framework continues to proliferate globally via community forks, including localized variations such as ScopeWeaver and a commercial version dubbed ARTEX PRO.

In a separate report, Check Point researchers showed AI agents in ARTEX control panels are running large-scale attacks with little human input for just a few hundred dollars, though they still fail and hallucinate successes.

Censys Uncovers ARTEX's Global Footprint

A report published on November 5 by Silas Cutler, principal security researcher at Censys Advanced Research Collective (ARC), has provided further insights into ARTEX's use and the infrastructure surrounding it.

The researcher found that 1465 hosts worldwide are exposing an ARTEX console to the public internet. About 650 of these hosts sit within two blocks of identically configured hosting, leaving roughly 815 distinct-looking deployments.

This suggests that ARTEX is not simply appearing on a handful of isolated systems, but across hundreds of seemingly distinct deployments worldwide, indicating a much broader footprint than initially reported.

Additionally, Censys telemetry showed that 155 internet-exposed ARTEX hosts (10.6%) also run at least one other artefact categorized by Censys as a threat.

These include other AI attack frameworks, reconnaissance platforms, tunneling tools and traditional malicious command-and-control (C2) servers such as Vshell, Cobalt Strike and Adaptix C2.

An asset-discovery and vulnerability-scanning platform dubbed ScopeSentry, which is maintained by the creator of ARTEX, is also listed by Censys as a threat artefact.

The researchers also found ARTEX sharing infrastructure with other popular AI-powered penetration-testing tools, including CyberStrikeAI, PentAGI, HexStrike AI and RedAmon. CyberStrikeAI, in particular, appeared alongside ARTEX on 70 hosts.

"Operators appear to be using multiple agent frameworks side by side," Cutler suggested.

Dutch-Belgian grocery giant Ahold Delhaize estimates that last month’s cyberattack, which disrupted operations in the US and the Benelux, will wipe €200 million to €250 million ($224 million to $280 million) off its fourth-quarter net sales.

The company, whose brands include Albert Heijn, Delhaize, Food Lion and Hannaford, published the estimate this week with its third-quarter results. The attack occurred after the quarter had closed.

The cybersecurity incident is also expected to cost Ahold Delhaize €75 million to €100 million ($84 million to $112 million) in fourth-quarter underlying and IFRS operating income. On top of that, the company faces incident response and remediation expenses, but believes these will have little effect on its IFRS operating income for 2026.

As a result, the retailer has revised its 2026 guidance downward. It now projects diluted underlying earnings per share, at constant exchange rates, to grow in the low single digits, rather than in the mid to high single digits it had previously forecast.

Free cash flow is now expected to reach around €2.1 billion ($2.36 billion), down from at least €2.3 billion ($2.58 billion). Ahold Delhaize attributes the reduction to the cyberattack and to newly introduced Serbian rules governing payments to suppliers.

The company first reported the incident in mid-October, announcing that it had disconnected some systems after detecting a security issue on its network. On October 19, it confirmed it had been hit by a cyberattack and said it had no evidence at the time that customer, associate or partner data had been stolen.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

“As part of our protocols to assess and mitigate cybersecurity incidents, we took some systems offline to help protect our IT environment. To differing degrees, this mainly affected our online capabilities in the Benelux and the U.S., as well as our Benelux supply-chain operations,” Frans Muller, Ahold Delhaize’s president and CEO, said in a statement accompanying the latest financial report.

“While most of the disruption was contained within two weeks, work continues to fully restore our normal operations,” he said.

Ahold Delhaize has yet to disclose what type of attack it experienced.

“While the cybersecurity incident has, understandably, demanded significant attention, it is important that we keep it in perspective. Our response demonstrates the resilience of our business; the incident does not define our business,” Muller said.

This is not the first time the company’s systems have been targeted. In November 2024, a ransomware attack disrupted several of its US brands, including Hannaford supermarkets and Giant Food pharmacies. The INC Ransom group claimed responsibility, and Ahold Delhaize later disclosed that the personal information of more than 2.2 million people had been compromised.

OpenSSH has rolled out emergency patches for a high-severity authentication bypass that allows attackers to log in using very long passwords.

Dubbed SSHole and tracked as CVE-2026-123158 (CVSS score of 8.1), the security defect affects the OpenSSH server (sshd) on Linux distributions that use the musl libc implementation with the Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) disabled.

A “misinterpretation of whether a string is intended to be a password hash” allows attackers to access certain accounts using any password that has between 257 and 1,024 characters.

Some accounts, such as root, should never accept a password, but in Linux distributions such as Alpine, OpenWrt, Buildroot, Yocto, and others, they do, Wakefield security researcher Özgün Kültekin says.

According to OpenSSH developer Damien Miller, the flaw is not in sshd itself, but can be exploited via sshd. Fixes were included in OpenSSH 10.6p2.

“We are making this release as fast as possible (we learned of the problem yesterday) because we have recently observed multiple cases of rapid bug rediscovery by AI agents, sometimes within hours, and so now consider long embargo periods to be a dangerous practice that primarily benefits attackers,” Miller said.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

On Thursday, Alpine Linux urged users to immediately apply the OpenSSH patches and restart sshd to replace the running daemon, or disable password logins and restart sshd.

“The attacker needs the name of an account whose password field is * (an account with no password set, which is normal for key-only accounts), and needs the machine to have at least one other account with a $5$ or $6$ password hash,” Alpine Linux warns.

Since version 3.16, Alpine Linux uses “*” to secure the root account, and $5$ or $6$ in password hashes show whether the SHA-256 or SHA-512 crypt was used.

“An attacker who can reach your SSH port can log in without knowing any password. It takes one connection, works every time, and needs no retries,” Alpine Linux notes.

Affected Alpine Linux deployments run OpenSSH without PAM, have password authentication enabled, have an account with the password field “*” (such as root, a key-only user created with adduser without a password, the alpine user in the official tiny-cloud images, or a user coming from a directory service through musl-nscd), and have at least one local account with a $5$ or $6$ password hash.

“Affected releases: every Alpine release we checked, 3.21 through 3.24 and edge, and the older releases that no longer receive regular updates (3.16 to 3.20),” Alpine Linux says.

“We haven’t seen any reports of exploitation yet, but the details are public, and the attack is simple, so I expect scanning to start within hours. Finding targets is very easy. Shodan lists around 22 million systems with SSH open on port 22, and the real number is higher because Shodan doesn’t see everything. Only some of those run Alpine, but each attempt is a single connection, so an attacker can afford to try all of them,” Detectify co-founder and principal security researcher Fredrik Almroth said.

“We’d be extremely surprised if we didn’t see SSH brute-forcers attempting this by the weekend. It’s virtually free to try and an easy win if it works. If your organization is affected, update to the latest version where possible, and disable password-based authentication as a temporary mitigation if you can’t,” WatchTowr head of threat intelligence Jake Knott said.

QNAP urges users to update Plex Media Server to the latest version available in the QNAP App Center, as hackers are exploiting the Plex2Shell vulnerability chain.

The vendor said it had received multiple reports of suspected compromises involving customers’ network-attached storage (NAS) devices.

"QNAP has received reports from some users that Plex Media Server on their NAS appears to have been compromised through [Plex2Shell] vulnerabilities, and QNAP Technical Support is assisting the affected users,” the company says in an advisory today.

Plex2Shell is a chain of four vulnerabilities in the Plex Media Server, tracked as CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655, and CVE-2026-96656.

Security researcher Zach Main discovered and reported the flaws to Plex on July 27. Exploitation started shortly after the full technical details became public on October 16.

CISA added all four flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 20, 2026, urging federal agencies to upgrade to Plex 1.43.3.10861 or later within three days, giving it maximum priority.

QNAP’s NAS devices are specialized computers with built-in storage that allow users to store, access, and share files across a network. They are typically used to back up computers and store media files.

Users can also expand their devices' capabilities by installing applications from the QNAP App Center, such as Plex Media Server, which streams movies, TV shows, and music directly from NAS drives.

QNAP advises users to update Plex Media Server to the latest version available through the QNAP App Center, currently 1.43.3.10861, to protect against Plex2Shell attacks.

“The QNAP Product Security Incident Response Team (QNAP PSIRT) has confirmed that the vulnerabilities exist only in Plex Media Server; QTS, QuTS hero, and other QNAP operating systems are not themselves affected,” the vendor says.

User action required

QNAP says that users should treat their NAS devices and all personal content as compromised if they're running a vulnerable Plex server that is exposed on the public web.

The vendor warned that updating now will not remove any payloads the attackers have already installed on the device.

The recommended action is to check for the signs of compromise shared in the security bulletin, perform a clean reinstall of the OS (QTS or QuTS hero), and then reset Plex and NAS credentials.

Users who do not need to access Plex remotely should disable the related features and stop forwarding port 32400. Those who need remote access are advised to connect via VPN.

QNAP has released a detailed step-by-step remediation guide on how to do the above.

The company also offers to investigate logs from suspected compromises, which users can submit via QNAP’s technical support portal.
