372d71761863.text:
Passwords and API keys that developers typed into commands they approved in Claude Code are sitting in public GitHub repositories, where anyone can read them.

When a user selects "Yes, and don't ask again," Anthropic's AI coding assistant can save the command, word-for-word, including the secret, in a project settings file.

Software security company Apiiro said yesterday that 1,122 public copies of that file hold at least one secret, though it did not test whether any still work. One company the researchers notified earlier this week confirmed its key had been live.

The file is .claude/settings.local.json. Removing it from a project does not undo the leak, because older versions stay in git history and in forks of the repository. The researchers' advice is to rotate first: change every password, token, and key the file has ever held, then clean up.

How a Secret Lands in the File

By default, Claude Code asks before it runs most shell commands. If the user picks "Yes, and don't ask again," it saves an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json inside the project, according to its permissions documentation. Matching commands then run without asking in later sessions.

The rule covers only what the prompt offered. Sometimes that is a pattern, such as npm test *, and sometimes one exact command. When it is the exact command, any password or token typed into it is saved too, in plain text.

In public files, the researchers found saved commands with the secret still inside, and they reproduced the behavior with the latest models, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1.

Claude Code tries to keep the file out of git. The first time it writes the file in a git repository, it adds the file to the user's global git excludes, its settings documentation says. Git on that computer then ignores the file in every repository.

That protection stays in one user's git settings on one computer. It does nothing for a file that was already committed, the researchers say. Claude Code never adds the file to the project's own .gitignore, so the protection does not travel with the project.

In 539 of the 1,105 repositories the researchers traced, a commit listing Claude as a co-author changed the file. They take this to mean Claude often commits the file itself.

What Apiiro Found

Apiiro's search of public GitHub found 104,185 copies of the file in 103,617 repositories, its research write-up shows. About 1.1% of them, or 1,122 copies, hold at least one secret. Together they hold 1,379 different secrets.

A value counted as a secret when it matched a known key format, or when a password or token sat beside the address of a public server. An AI reviewer also had to agree. The researchers do not say whether anyone has used these secrets.

More than a third of the secrets open a database directly, including 379 database passwords. Others include 43 SSH logins for public servers, 42 tokens for GitHub, GitLab and npm, and 23 AWS keys.

Among the owners of these files are 63 organizations, mostly software companies of all sizes. The strongest cases include a database vendor's own admin-level cloud key and the owner password of a medical-records database, the researchers say.

As of Monday, every file with a secret was still on its repository's default branch, and in half of those repositories it had been there for at least 217 days.

Older versions of the file contain 734 more secrets across 509 repositories that are not present in any current copy, usually because the file was deleted. Forks spread the files further: 211 forks of 74 repositories carry the same secrets as the originals.

Secrets also sit in 298 of 76,011 copies of the shared .claude/settings.json file, which teams commit on purpose, mostly inside allow rules. Including those, the older versions, and saved agent chat logs, the total is 2,539 secrets across 1,994 repositories.

Of 16 coding agents whose documentation the researchers compared, Claude Code is the only one confirmed to save the full approved command in a project file by default.

What to Do

For developers, the researchers recommend these steps:

Search your GitHub organization for .claude/settings.local.json and .claude/settings.json, and check each repository's git history for them, even where the files are gone.

Rotate every password, token and key the files have ever held, before cleaning up.

Stop tracking the local file with git rm --cached .claude/settings.local.json, and add it to the repository's own .gitignore.

Open the file on your own computer, even if it was never committed, and delete every rule that contains a secret.

Keep secrets out of commands. Refer to them as variables from a secrets manager, such as $DB_URL, so the saved rule holds the variable name and not the secret.

Approve patterns, such as Bash(npm run:*), instead of single commands.

Copies that never reach GitHub still matter, the researchers say. The file is plain JSON in the project folder, and it can also be left inside an npm package, a Docker image, a zip archive, or a synced folder.

Malware has previously looked for secrets on developer machines. In September 2025, the Shai-Hulud worm ran the TruffleHog secret scanner over infected computers, and the scanner flagged more than half of the files as secret.

Common secret scanners miss many of these files. The researchers ran gitleaks and TruffleHog over every copy, without the tools' verification step. Of the 1,122 files with a secret, gitleaks flagged 564 and TruffleHog 643, and neither flagged 215.

Most misses are passwords typed inside commands. Scanners look for known key formats, and a password after PGPASSWORD=, sshpass -p , or mysql -p looks like an ordinary word in an ordinary command line.

For security teams, the researchers recommend:

Treat agent folders such as .claude/, .cursor/, .gemini/ and .specstory/, and agent memory files, as holding secrets, like .env files, on laptops as well as in repositories.

Add them to pre-commit and CI secret scanning, including git history, and make sure the scanner catches passwords inside commands, not only known key formats.

Add .claude/settings.local.json to the organization's .gitignore templates.

Check credentials paired with a public server first, because those are the ones that give access.

Earlier Reports

Claude Code users have reported this behavior before. An earlier bug report, filed on August 11, 2025, said approved commands with API keys and tokens were being stored word for word in settings.local.json.

An automated bot closed that report as "not planned" on January 3, after 60 days without activity.

As of today, the four related reports the researchers cite have all been closed by the same bot, the most recent yesterday. None got a reply from Anthropic, they say.

de9d6392395c.text: NHS staff drafted into a helpline after colleagues' health data was exposed online faced distressed callers, safeguarding concerns, and a "serious emotional impact," a review has found. The report [PDF] comes almost exactly a year after the Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust disclosed a data breach affecting 8,003 people, including current and former trust staff and non-trust workers. A member of the public discovered the exposure in November 2025. An Excel workbook published in response to a Freedom of Information request in February 2023 retained underlying sickness absence records that users could reveal through its pivot tables. Staff assigned to the helpline described difficult calls involving shouting, anger, and distress. Particularly difficult calls involved people distressed by the sensitivity of the disclosures or potentially in danger from domestic abuse. Call handlers said they had to make safeguarding assessments without training or an established process. "Such occurrences of anger or distress were not infrequent, and this reflected the heightened emotions and distress experienced by callers to varying degrees due to the breach," the review noted. "This placed significant emotional burden on individuals working in the contact center, who were not prepared or provided support on how to deal with those." Members of the trust's clinical governance team were told just a day beforehand that they would staff the helpline. Despite their experience dealing with patient trauma, they received little preparation for the calls that followed. "The staff working in the call centers had a short training session and then the calls started coming in within minutes of the team being set up," the review noted. "Some staff had not finished reading the pre-prepared script which had arrived only 30 minutes before the center went live." Most call handlers only learned that their own data had been exposed while already working on the helpline, sometimes minutes before supporting others affected. Call handlers also said they had little choice about taking on the work and were expected to maintain their usual duties alongside it. The review stated that some staff members gave up weekends and worked long past their scheduled hours to meet the demands of both roles. "It's typical NHS, it runs on goodwill," one staffer told the team that compiled the report. The call center was only supposed to run for two weeks in December 2025, but due to the volume of calls, it was eventually stood down after 11 weeks, in February 2026. According to officials speaking at a trust board meeting on Thursday, the review and its findings have since been circulated among staff, and published online. How the spreadsheet slipped through Responding to a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request thought to be from a journalist researching a story about stress in the NHS, the Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust uploaded a spreadsheet to its public FOI Disclosure log in February 2023. This contained personal data and inadvertently exposed sickness absence information and sensitive health data related to 7,715 staff, 288 non-trust workers, as well as a small number of unidentified records. Crucially, this spreadsheet was uploaded in a format that allowed users to access the pivot table from which some data was derived. The data in these pivot tables would normally have been too sensitive to be included in FOIA responses. The first failure was that the request was handled by the trust's e-Rostering team instead of the People Information Unit, which had the expertise in responding to FOIA requests with complex datasets. The e-Rostering team compiled the response using the team's own data, but incorrectly believed they had stripped the spreadsheet of the sensitive data that would later be exposed. Standard procedures instructed request handlers to follow several steps to ensure sensitive data was stripped before documents are published, some of which were skipped. For starters, one FOI officer assigned to the response either failed to run the spreadsheet through Excel's Document Inspector, which formed part of the usual procedures, or failed to act upon its recommendations. This feature can flag pivot tables and potentially hidden cached data, but cannot determine whether that data is sensitive or automatically remove the cache. Staff also failed to follow instructions to convert the spreadsheet to PDF. Investigators found that doing so prevented users clicking through to the underlying records, although they could not guarantee that no hidden data remained technically accessible. At the time, internal guidance did not require conversion to CSV, which would have removed the workbook's pivot-table functionality and embedded cache. The trust's sign-off process also focused on answering the request's questions and meeting their public relations duties, and falsely assumed that the data had been adequately sanitized before the final review. The spreadsheet was made available for 33 months, although the trust is not sure how many times it was viewed during that time. Its logs only covered the 12 months before a member of the public alerted it to the pivot table issue. These indicated that it had been accessed 340 times, although the review noted there was no way of knowing how many of these, if any, led to pivot tables being accessed, or even if it was viewed by a human, with web crawlers adding to the total view count. The trust has since implemented a number of changes to prevent a recurrence of the breach, including the mandatory password-protecting of any Excel workbook as part of FOIA responses. A senior information governance officer must now approve spreadsheet responses before executive sign-off. Revised guidance circulated in November 2025 also called for conversion to CSV, although investigators found that this requirement had not been incorporated into the formal operating procedure and recommended updating it. The review says the Information Commissioner's Office closed its case after the trust implemented its recommendations. A spokesperson for the Royal Cornwall Hospitals said: "We are deeply sorry for the accidental sharing of sickness absence data which we reported in November 2025, and for the distress and concern it caused those colleagues whose data was involved. "An independent investigation has now been completed, and the report has been published in full on our website in the interests of transparency and accountability. "The investigation has helped us understand what happened and identify areas where improvements were needed. We have already implemented a number of measures to strengthen our processes, particularly around the management of Freedom of Information requests and responses. "The protection of personal information is of the utmost importance to us, and we remain committed to learning from this incident and preventing a similar event from happening again. "We continue to provide support to colleagues who have been affected." ®

a535baf3ec1f.text:
SonicWall has patched a SonicOS vulnerability that can be used to bypass SAML authentication, warning customers that it may have been exploited in attacks.

Tracked as CVE-2026-19868, the flaw affects the SSL VPN component of SonicOS, the operating system that runs on SonicWall firewalls. It’s one of seven vulnerabilities described in an advisory published on November 6.

“An authentication enforcement vulnerability in SonicOS SSLVPN service may allow a user with valid credentials for an alternate authentication method to bypass SAML authentication controls. Successful exploitation may also bypass SAML-enforced multi-factor authentication (MFA),” reads SonicWall’s description of CVE-2026-19868.

According to the vendor, an SSL VPN is exposed only if SAML-based login is enabled. CVE-2026-19868 has a CVSS score of 7.1, which puts it in the high-severity range. The flaw was reported by Ryan Harris of The Electronic Office.

SonicWall said its product security team “has investigated a report indicating potential exploitation of this vulnerability.”

CISA added CVE-2026-19868 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on the same day. Under Binding Operational Directive 26-04, federal agencies must address it by November 20.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Neither the vendor nor CISA has shared any details about the suspected attacks. It’s also unclear whether the flaw was exploited as a zero-day, before a patch became available.

Impacted devices include Gen7 TZ, NSa, NSsp and NSv firewalls with SonicOS 7.3.3-7015 or older. Gen8 TZ, NSa and NSv firewalls with SonicOS 8.2.2-8015 or older are also affected.

SonicOS versions 7.3.4-7013 and 8.2.3-8015 resolve the issue, and there are no workarounds. “Customers are strongly urged to upgrade to the latest release as soon as possible to mitigate the associated risks,” SonicWall said.

SonicWall’s advisory doesn’t mark any of the other six flaws as exploited. Two of them, each with a CVSS score of 8.8, affect the SonicOS management interface. One is a permissive cross-domain policy issue and the other is a session validation bug.

Under certain circumstances, a remote attacker could abuse either one without logging in to take unauthorized actions.

Three of the remaining flaws are pre-authentication buffer overflows in the SSL VPN service and the TACACS+ authentication client. Attackers could use them to launch DoS attacks at the application level.

The last one is a weak password hashing issue in virtual appliances. An attacker who already has high-privileged local access could exploit it to obtain a platform credential, which gives access to some of the platform’s settings.

Threat actors often exploit SonicWall product vulnerabilities. CISA’s KEV catalog currently includes 20 security holes, but the agency has yet to add CVE-2026-102255, which hackers started targeting last month, just days after its disclosure.

Related: Cisco, WatchGuard Release Patches; SonicWall Won’t Fix GMS Flaws

Related: SonicWall Warns of Two SMA1000 Zero-Days Exploited in Attacks

Related: SonicWall and Splunk Patch Critical Vulnerabilities

This week, we are joined by Matt Poto, Associate Triage Analyst at Huntress, discussing their work on "Grand Theft Auto VI Hype Leads to Malware." Threat actors are exploiting the hype surrounding the upcoming release of Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA6) by distributing fake leaked game downloads designed to infect unsuspecting gamers.

Huntress identified malicious ISOs promoted through search engine poisoning, gaming forums, torrent sites, and social media that contain multiple types of malware, including remote access trojans (RATs), an infostealer, and ransomware. The malware can steal credentials and personal information, give attackers control of compromised systems, and encrypt or destroy files, with evidence suggesting the campaign may be targeting Russian-speaking gamers.

The research and executive brief can be found here:

⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠Grand Theft Auto VI Hype Leads to Malware

In this article

Mitigation and protection guidance

Microsoft Defender detections

Hunting queries

Indicators of compromise

In October 2026, the financially motivated threat actor Storm-3358 began targeting organizations in the financial sector using the agentic AI offensive framework ARTEX. The threat actor that Microsoft Threat Intelligence tracks as Storm-3358 is a Cambodia-based intrusion cluster that primarily targets financial organizations in Southeast Asia, in addition to a smaller number of large financial organizations globally.

Microsoft has observed Storm-3358 use ARTEX in combination with conventional automated tools to scan systems connected to the public internet, exploit security flaws including anonymous file upload and server-side request forgery (SSRF), and install open-source remote access trojans (RATs). Storm-3358 has used the WISP, vshell, and AdaptixC2 RATs for persistence and lateral movement. Microsoft has observed ARTEX agents using utilities like netcat and curl to download these RATs to compromised systems, as shown in Figure 1.

Figure 1. Example commands that ARTEX agents used to download RATs to compromised systems.

In recent ARTEX-related attacks, threat actors have used ARTEX agents to scan and exploit vulnerabilities in web applications, use web shells for persistence on compromised web servers, compromise credentials from public sources and compromised systems, and use compromised cloud identities for persistence and data exfiltration. ARTEX agents can also perform brute-force password attacks, password spraying, API enumeration and abuse, and database dumping. Agentic tools like ARTEX can leverage compromised credentials and systems at machine speed to move laterally, escalate privileges, and exfiltrate data.

This activity illustrates an ongoing trend of threat actors accelerating all stages of the attack chain with agentic AI penetration testing frameworks, including ARTEX. As these capabilities evolve, defenders must similarly use AI to investigate and respond across large environments.

While threat actors regularly use proxies and virtual private networks (VPNs) to change the source IP address of malicious traffic and bypass static detections, Microsoft is providing indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help defenders detect related activity.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Microsoft’s research into threats involving agentic frameworks informs security detections and investigative context across its products. The capabilities available to customers depend on the source of the activity and the products and protections deployed in their environment.

Several behavioral signals can help organizations determine that they are being targeted by threat actors using agentic AI. Agentic AI frameworks scanning a target send a wide variety of requests in a brief time and retry variations on the same technique or move on to next-stage actions at machine speed. Agentic AI frameworks use existing penetration testing tools. For example, ARTEX by default uses Nmap, curl, wget, Python HTTP clients, Norma SDK WebFetch, and headless Chromium through Playwright, among others. These tools may send network traffic with distinctive characteristics, such as default user agent strings. While blocking network traffic with these characteristics will not stop an attack by an AI agent, which will quickly change them, identifying them can alert defenders to the activity.

Defensive honeypots, decoys, tarpits, and fake wins can pull autonomous AI attacks away from legitimate targets. Honeypots and decoy surfaces such as Microsoft Sentinel Deception give the agent attractive but worthless targets to pursue. Tarpits consume the agent’s time and budget. Fake wins present convincing evidence that the agent’s objective is complete, which can cause it to stop on a false success. In Microsoft’s testing, these controls helped reduce the attack traffic reaching real assets and produced high-confidence, attribution-quality signal.

For additional information on the evolution of threat actors’ use of ARTEX please see Microsoft’s recent blogs: AI-driven, large-scale nation-state campaign using ARTEX enables supply chain compromise and Threat actors use agentic AI tooling to find and abuse exposed secrets.

Microsoft’s continuous research into threat actors leveraging agentic frameworks integrates directly into the following products:

Identity and sign-in activity — Microsoft Entra ID Protection

Microsoft analyzes sign-in activity and other signals to identify potential identity risk. Customers can investigate risk detections and risky sign-ins, and configure Conditional Access policies that use sign-in or user risk to require multifactor authentication or block access when specified conditions are met. Identity and sign-in activity from known threat actor infrastructure, including from agentic frameworks like ARTEX, generate Verified threat actor IP risk detections delivered at high risk. See:

Investigate risk with Microsoft Entra ID Protection

Risk-based user sign-in protection in Microsoft Entra ID

What are risk detections? – Microsoft Entra ID Protection

Endpoint activity — Microsoft Defender for Endpoint

Endpoint alerts help security teams identify and investigate suspicious activity on devices. Indicators of compromise can support detection and, when configured, blocking. Customers can review related alerts in the Microsoft Defender portal. See:

Review alerts in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint

Activity across security domains — Microsoft Defender portal

The portal brings together alerts and incidents from Microsoft security solutions and provides relevant threat intelligence to support investigation, threat hunting, and response. This helps customers assess suspicious activity in the context of their own environment. See:

Investigate alerts in Microsoft Defender XDR

Security Dashboard for AI

Threat actor misuse of AI accelerates risk across enterprise environments by amplifying existing threats such as exploitation of vulnerabilities, phishing, malware threats, and insider activity. To help organizations stay ahead of AI-enabled threat activity, Microsoft has introduced the Security Dashboard for AI. The dashboard provides users with a unified view of AI security posture by aggregating security, identity, and data risk across Microsoft Defender, Microsoft Entra, and Microsoft Purview. See:

Today, Huntress Managed SIEM's Brute Force Sentry is available to all Managed SIEM customers. It turns the brute force attacks our SOC sees in the field into detections that fire earlier, with the evidence and hardening guidance you need to close the gap. Brute Force Sentry watches your internet-facing login surfaces, including RDP, RD Gateway, and the RDWeb portal on Windows and SSH on Linux. When a run of failed logons ends in a successful one, the Huntress SOC investigates.

Every exposed login gets knocked on, and most of that knocking is bots cycling through "administrator" on a gateway someone set up years ago. The trouble is that one burst out of thousands ends in a working login, and a generic threshold rule treats it the same as the rest.

Brute Force Sentry is built to find that one.

RDP is still a front door attackers use

Huntress research ties RDP to 10–20% of how advanced attackers break into networks. Plenty of organizations don't realize their RDWeb portal or RD Gateway is reachable from the internet until someone starts working through usernames on it.

RDWeb and RD Gateway behave a lot like an SSL VPN portal. Authentication happens at the web portal, before the user ever reaches an endpoint, so that portal is where attackers line up.

Most SIEMs handle brute force with a single threshold rule, something like "X failed logons in Y minutes." Set it low and your team drowns in alerts from bots that never get in. Set it high and a slow spray across dozens of accounts slips right under it. In both cases, the rule can't answer the question you care about: did one of those attempts work?

How Brute Force Sentry works

Brute Force Sentry reads the authentication telemetry your Managed SIEM already collects across all three platforms: Windows Security events (4624, 4625, 4740, 4776) and RD Gateway's own connection log, Linux sshd, and macOS, and splits "brute force" into the distinct tradecraft it really is:

Traditional brute force: one source guessing against a few accounts until something works

Distributed brute force: many sources working the same account, each staying quiet enough on its own to look unremarkable

Spraying: a short list of common credentials tried across many accounts

Credential stuffing: username and password pairs from earlier breaches, tested to see which still work

Username enumeration: repeated attempts against accounts that don't exist, probing for valid names before the guessing starts

It reads each platform in its own language. Windows spreads a single authentication across several event IDs, with the failure reason buried in a status code and the credential check sometimes landing on a domain controller instead of the machine being attacked. Linux writes one sshd line that already separates a wrong password from an attempt against an account that was never real. Rather than flatten both into a lowest common denominator, we normalize them into one authentication record that keeps what each platform knows, so the detection logic is identical everywhere and nothing is lost in translation.

It's tuned per surface, not set once.. Each one gets its own narrow correlation detection in place of a single noisy rule. Our researchers tuned every detection per login surface against historical partner data, then validated it against simulated real-world attacks in the lab before the SOC got it.

It correlates across providers. The failed sign-ins and the success that follows are often recorded by two different systems on the same host. Brute Force Sentry normalizes both into one authentication surface, so a single detection can follow the attack from the first failure to the login.

It turns itself on, and tells you when it can't. Brute Force Sentry activates per organization once the telemetry it needs is flowing. If that telemetry is missing, it shows as unavailable along with the reason, so a quiet dashboard means Huntress checked and found nothing.

The accounts they go after aren't the ones you're watching

Across the compromises Huntress has worked, the accounts that fell weren't always domain admins. They were the ones nobody owns; shared logins created for a device, a front desk, or a one off integration, with a password nobody has rotated since and an MFA exemption nobody remembers granting. They don't surface on a privileged-account review, and they don't belong to anyone who'd notice them being used. That's exactly why attackers reach for them first, and the pattern holds whichever door they come through: a Windows desktop or gateway, a Linux server, or a Mac sharing its screen.

Brute Force Sentry surfaces the usernames being attempted, not just how many times. That includes the ones that don't exist. A run of failures against accounts that were never real is username enumeration, someone working a list, learning your naming convention before they start guessing passwords in earnest. Catching that tells you an attack is being set up rather than already underway. And seeing which real accounts an attacker keeps returning to tell you which credentials to rotate tonight, not next quarter.

About 1,700 attempts in 72 seconds

In June 2026, the Huntress SOC handled a compromise at an organization running Remote Desktop Gateway. The attacker hit eight accounts with 212 to 215 failed logons each, roughly 1,700 attempts in 72 seconds, and then got in.

Every one of those failures was sitting in the gateway host's event logs. The successful login that came right after was recorded by RD Gateway, a different provider on the same host. Connecting the two took a detection that didn't exist yet, and Brute Force Sentry was built to make that connection.

To see how often this pattern shows up, we reviewed 30 confirmed RDWeb/RDG compromises during the first four weeks of testing. In 20 of them, Brute Force Sentry's signal would have reached the SOC up to an hour earlier. That's an hour between the attacker's first guess and their first move inside the network, and it's an hour our analysts can spend containing the account.

An attacker who gets in through your gateway keeps moving, so the sooner you see the login, the less of the network they've touched.

What you'll see in the portal

Most brute force activity never succeeds, and until now partners haven't seen any of it. Brute Force Sentry shows it as it happens, so you can act on your own terms before something breaks through:

Exposed surfaces: which internet-facing login surfaces are under attack, including ones you may not have known were reachable

Targeted accounts: the accounts attackers keep coming back to

Sources: where the attempts come from, and which sources keep returning

Compromises: successful logins that followed a run of failures, each linked to its Incident Report

You're notified on compromise, and you can opt in to notifications for every attempt, successful or not.

Figure 1: Brute Force Sentry dashboard

Less noise for you, more proof for your customers

If you're an MSP, you've probably told a client their RD Gateway needs MFA or belongs behind a VPN. Brute Force Sentry gives you their own data to make that case, starting with whether the portal should be exposed at all: which accounts were targeted last week, how many attempts were made, and where they came from. Pair that with the hardening guidance in each finding, and the conversation moves from "we should" to "here's what happened."

Internal IT teams get the same benefit. You don't have to become a Windows event log specialist to tell whether a burst of 4625s was background noise or the start of an intrusion, because the Huntress SOC is already looking at the ones that matter.

Built from the attacks our SOC works

Brute Force Sentry started with a real incident and a gap our analysts could name. That's how we want Managed SIEM to keep growing: take the attacks our SOC sees in partner environments and turn them into detections that fire earlier, with the evidence attached.

Every exposed login gets knocked on. Now you'll know which knock got answered.

Already on Huntress Managed SIEM? It's included for all Managed SIEM customers and turns on automatically once your Windows authentication telemetry is flowing. New to Managed SIEM? Book a demo to see Brute Force Sentry and the Huntress SOC in action.

SonicWall has released security updates to fix seven vulnerabilities in SonicOS firewalls, including an SSL-VPN authentication bypass flaw exploited in attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-19868, allows attackers with valid credentials for an alternate authentication method to bypass SAML authentication controls, potentially including SAML-enforced multi-factor authentication (MFA).

The flaw has a CVSS severity score of 7.1 and only affects SonicOS SSL-VPN services configured to use SAML authentication.

In a security advisory published Friday, SonicWall warned that it had investigated a report that the vulnerability was exploited in an attack and urged customers to install the latest security updates.

"SonicWall PSIRT has investigated a report indicating potential exploitation of this vulnerability. Customers are strongly urged to upgrade to the latest release as soon as possible to mitigate the associated risks," the company warned.

Ryan Harris of The Electronic Office discovered and reported the vulnerability.

While SonicWall has not shared details about the reported exploitation, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added CVE-2026-19868 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, confirming that the flaw has been exploited in the wild.

CISA ordered federal civilian executive branch agencies to secure affected systems by November 20, 2026.

The advisory also fixes six additional vulnerabilities in SonicOS, including two management interface flaws rated 8.8 severity that allow unauthenticated attackers to perform unauthorized operations under specific conditions.

The remaining flaws include pre-authentication buffer overflows in the SSL-VPN and TACACS+ services that could cause denial-of-service conditions, and a weak password hashing vulnerability affecting virtual appliances.

The vulnerabilities affect SonicOS Gen7 versions 7.3.3-7015 and earlier and Gen8 versions 8.2.2-8015 and earlier. SonicWall fixed the issues in versions 7.3.4-7013 and 8.2.3-8015 and says no workarounds are available.

The warning comes after a series of attacks targeting SonicWall's SMA1000 secure remote access appliances.

In October, security researchers detected exploitation attempts targeting CVE-2026-102255, a maximum-severity vulnerability that could allow unauthenticated attackers to access internal functionality and perform unauthorized operations.

Those attempts followed September attacks that chained two SMA1000 zero-days to achieve remote code execution, as well as July attacks that exploited two other zero-days to deploy malware on vulnerable appliances.

Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

Amid an onslaught of AI vulnerability discovery and AI-assisted hacking, some of the most consequential critical infrastructure attacks this year may have little to do with the technology at all—instead providing a stark reminder that cybersecurity fundamentals are still key to digital defense.

Three sites in France that handle blood and plasma bags were briefly impacted this week by widespread attacks on vulnerable internet-connected refrigerators. On Wednesday, the Établissement Français du Sang (EFS) confirmed that cold rooms storing blood were “raised to very high temperatures” on November 2. The blood samples, thankfully, weren’t altered or damaged, the EFS said, because the organization’s alarm facilities and staff quickly detected the changes and implemented fail-safe measures.

The incident, however, comes amid a wave of cyberattacks in recent days affecting supermarket chains in at least 11 European countries that also drastically increased the temperatures of their refrigerators. Pictures from across the continent show huge volumes of food being trashed following the spikes. Similar fridge attacks in October affected hundreds of French stores that were forced to throw away food. And in August, roughly six commissaries and grocery stores on United States military bases suffered similar incidents resulting in spoiled food. The Pentagon is investigating the incidents and is collaborating with French law enforcement, Reuters reported last week.

“It's been true for more than a decade now that our dependence on connected technology is growing faster than our collective will to protect it, which has exposed us to accidents, adversaries, and now potentially agents,” says longtime critical infrastructure researcher Josh Corman, who is currently the executive in residence for public safety and resilience at the nonprofit Institute for Security and Technology. “These fragile cold-chain systems are too critical to fail, but we keep experiencing hard lessons.”

It is still unclear who is behind the incidents and whether the attacks are all connected or being carried out by multiple actors. The first recent wave of attacks against French supermarkets last month appears to have been caused by attackers exploiting unpatched refrigeration controllers exposed to the internet—including software versions that allegedly used weak passwords formulated based on the date.

Many of the hacks stem from attackers exploiting vulnerabilities in temperature controllers made by the Danish firm Danfoss, and researchers say the attacks would not have been particularly difficult to pull off. Danfoss did not return WIRED’s request for comment.

French cooperative bank Crédit Mutuel Arkéa was targeted in a cyberattack that enabled fraudulent transactions of up to $133 million, forcing it to respond by suspending certain systems.

The bank says that the attacker used its own account to initiate transactions to other banking organizations, but customer assets remain unaffected.

Crédit Mutuel Arkéa is a major French banking group with more than 5.8 million members and 211.5 billion euros in assets.

Reports about the incident emerged on November 2, initially from blockchain fraud investigator ZachXBT, who warned of a large-scale unauthorized withdrawal from multiple centralized exchange accounts occurring a day earlier.

According to the investigator, the attacker may have stolen up to 118 million euros ($133 million) and withdrawn it as USDC and USDT stablecoins.

At the time, ZachXBT did not name the entity but said that the lack of public disclosure allowed the attacker to launder $30 million by November 3, which EU law enforcement would otherwise have frozen.

Crédit Mutuel Arkéa disclosed the incident on November 4, assuring customers that it “is now closed and under control” and that operations are gradually returning to normal.

“Crédit Mutuel Arkéa wishes to reassure all its clients - across its federations and subsidiaries - that this incident has no impact on their assets; it has merely resulted in a delay in the execution of certain transfer transactions,” [machine translated] the bank stated.

However, the organization also warned of increased phishing risk, urging customers to stay vigilant against unsolicited communications and avoid sharing sensitive details over the phone or email.

All suspicious messages should be verified by calling the bank adviser directly.

In a separate FAQ page, the bank explained that the attacker reached its network directly through a service provider’s platform, but ruled out Fortuneo.

The attacker then used Arkéa’s own account, not customers' accounts, to transact with other banking institutions and convert funds into cryptocurrency.

While the bank did not confirm ZachXBT's estimation of the stolen amount, it acknowledged that the amount was significant and some funds were blocked.

"Do you confirm that 118 million euros (133 million dollars) were stolen? We do not confirm this information and can only validate the order of magnitude."

Arkéa ruled out human error at the bank and instead described the incident as a "sophisticated attack."

The bank is currently working with judicial authorities and the police to establish the attack’s exact origin and modus operandi.

BleepingComputer has contacted Crédit Mutuel Arkéa to learn more about the attack and the status of investigations, but we have not received a response yet.

Fraudulent reward portals and fake gift card giveaways are surging globally, tricking users into deceptive verification loops and paid subscriptions.

These scams lure victims with a simple pitch: click an ad featuring a celebrity endorsement, claim a free gift card from a well-known brand, and complete a quick "human verification" step to unlock the reward.

Read the full report here: https://www.ctm360.com/reports/gift-card-scams

Behind the polished branding, fake progress bars, and convincing promotional messages, however, no actual gift cards are provided.

Instead, these campaigns operate as large-scale affiliate monetization schemes designed to collect personal information, generate application installs, and enroll unsuspecting users in recurring mobile subscriptions.

1,000+ Incidents Exploiting Trusted Brands

Based on activity observed by CTM360, analysts identified more than 1,000 incidents linked to this recurring campaign.

Threat actors exploit consumer familiarity with established brands, frequently impersonating major retailers and consumer platforms such as PlayStation, Sephora, SHEIN, Walmart, and Amazon.

To increase credibility and attract potential victims, the campaigns rely heavily on social media distribution through:

Sponsored social media ads

Viral posts promoting "giveaways"

Fabricated endorsements from high-profile celebrities and influencers (such as MrBeast or Alix Earle)

Because the underlying infrastructure is highly modular, threat actors can swap out the impersonated brand, celebrity lure, and domain name without rebuilding the core scam engine.

How the Campaign Works: The Fake Generation Trap

CTM360 maps this activity using a structured fraud lifecycle, highlighting how victims are systematically pushed through a psychological progression of curiosity, trust, and urgency.

Once a user clicks a malicious ad, they are redirected to a fraudulent reward portal.

To appear credible, these websites display:

Cloned brand logos and colors

Fake participant numbers and live countdown timers

Fabricated testimonials from "recent winners"

After a victim selects a gift card value, the site runs a scripted, visual progress animation simulating the generation of the card on the back end.

The portal then displays a partially masked code (e.g., XXXX-XXXX-7F3A-XXXX) to convince the user that the reward is real and ready to claim.

Before the full code is revealed, the victim is presented with a deceptive "Security Check" or "Human Verification" gate.

Download The Gift Card Scam Report

Discover how threat actors use brand impersonation and fake rewards to exploit users.

Get insights into attacker infrastructure and learn to defend your organization with CTM360's Digital Risk Protection.

Download Now

The Endless Verification Loop and Monetization

The "human verification" step is a deceptive pivot into what CTM360 identifies as "Trap 10." Rather than performing a legitimate security check, the verification process redirects victims to third-party activities designed to generate revenue for the operators.

Victims are pushed into an endless loop of:

Completing surveys, quizzes, and promotional offers.

Installing unwanted third-party applications or browser extensions.

Subscribing to paid mobile services through localized carrier-billing mechanisms

If a user completes a task, they are not given the gift card. The site simply reports the step as "incomplete" and pushes the victim to another offer. In all flows tested by CTM360, no reward was ever delivered.

Technical Observations: Affiliate Hand-Offs

Unlike traditional phishing that steals user credentials, this campaign operates on a volume-and-conversion model.

CTM360 observed that lure pages redirect victims through affiliate tracking URLs (e.g., passing parameters like offer_id and aff_id). This tracking token links the victim's registration directly to the threat actor's affiliate network account.

When a victim completes a mobile number submission and PIN/OTP verification for a subscription, the threat actor earns a commission.

Risks to Users and Organizations

For the victim, the fallout goes beyond wasted time. Consequences include personal information exposure, unexpected mobile billing charges, and an influx of spam.

For organizations, this represents a severe abuse of brand reputation. The campaign highlights a broader trend: attackers are operating at scale, weaponizing brand trust as a mechanism to drive lucrative affiliate conversions.

A critical flaw in Ruby on Rails could allow an unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files on an app's server by uploading a crafted file if the app processes uploads using ImageMagick. The Rails project disclosed the flaw in an advisory and fixed it in versions 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2.

The flaw is in Active Storage, the part of Rails that handles file uploads. Some apps store uploaded files using Active Storage's Disk service, which stores them on the server's disk. In those apps, an attacker could also read any file the app can read.

Those files typically include the app's secret_key_base and its credentials for other systems, according to Rails. Reading them may in turn allow remote code execution or lateral movement into those systems.

Rails rates the flaw 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale. It is tracked as GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9 and does not yet have a CVE identifier.

ImageMagick selects a format handler, which it calls a coder, based on the file's content. Some coders act on other files named inside the image, not on the image itself. Active Storage imposes no limits on which coders an upload can use, so the server's own ImageMagick policy was the only limit.

The ImageMagick analyzer in Active Storage runs when a file is attached. Attaching the upload is enough to reach the flaw. The app does not have to make a variant (a transformed copy of the image) or a preview, or call analyze.

An uploaded SVG file reached ImageMagick's MSL coder through that analyzer, according to the commit that fixed the flaw. MSL is a scripting coder that reads and writes files named by its script.

Rails said one attack chain was reported to it, but it does "not assume it is the only one that exists." The advisory does not say whether the flaw has been exploited.

The flaw was reported through HackerOne by RyotaK, a researcher at GMO Flatt Security.

Which Rails Apps Are Affected

An app is affected only if all three of these are true:

It uses ImageMagick for Active Storage image processing. That is the setting config.active_storage.variant_processor = :mini_magick, the default for apps on load_defaults 6.1 or earlier.

Its ImageMagick security policy does not already block the coders involved. Rails says the policies that Debian and Ubuntu ship do not.

It accepts file uploads from untrusted users.

To check the first condition, look at config.active_storage.variant_processor. If it is not set, the default depends on load_defaults: :mini_magick before 7.0, and :vips from 7.0 on. The same setting decides which library analyzes uploads, not only which one makes variants.

Every Active Storage version before 8.0.5.2 is affected, as are 8.1 versions before 8.1.4.1. Release series older than 8.0 are no longer supported, and Rails will not release fixed versions for them.

In July, Rails fixed a different critical Active Storage flaw, CVE-2026-66066, which affected apps that use libvips instead of ImageMagick. Apps using ImageMagick were not exposed to that flaw's attack path, but they can be exposed to this one.

The same releases fix a second Active Storage flaw, GHSA-v924-7rp8-4mxh, which Rails rates high with a CVSS score of 8.8. Active Storage passed uploads to ImageMagick and FFmpeg under temporary file names that kept the uploaded file's extension.

Those tools can pick a decoder from the extension when a file's content does not show its format. So an attacker who chose an upload's filename and declared its content type could choose the decoder that processes it.

What to Do

Rails strongly recommends upgrading as soon as possible. The two releases fix 21 security issues in total.

The fixed versions ship an ImageMagick security policy. MiniMagick is the Ruby gem Active Storage uses to call ImageMagick. In its default setup, every ImageMagick command it runs applies the policy, not only commands from Active Storage.

The policy blocks the MSL coder; coders that read or delete files other than the image; coders that fetch remote or local references or display them on a screen; every coder backed by Ghostscript, along with the gs delegate; and @filename indirection.

Upgrade to Rails 8.1.4.1 or 8.0.5.2. Apps on :mini_magick also need mini_magick 5.1 or later, or they raise an error at boot. Rails 8.0 gets security fixes only until November 7, 2026, under its maintenance policy.

Confirm that the app loads the new policy, as the Active Storage guide describes, by running bin/rails runner 'puts MiniMagick.identify { |i| i.list "policy" }'.

Check whether the shipped policy reaches the app at all. It does not reach an app that replaces MiniMagick.cli_env after boot, clears the environment with MiniMagick.cli_prefix, or installs its own MiniMagick::Shell. Such an app must put the rules in ImageMagick's system policy.

Apps that use GraphicsMagick get no protection from the shipped policy, because GraphicsMagick does not read ImageMagick policies.

Check the server's own ImageMagick policy. The shipped policy adds to it rather than replacing it. A rule there that allows a coder, including a wildcard such as pattern="*", overrides the shipped policy's block on that coder.

If the app renders PDF or PostScript files through ImageMagick, re-allow the gs delegate and the coders it uses in the server's policy.xml.

If you cannot upgrade yet, copy the rules of the shipped policy, activestorage/lib/active_storage/image_magick/policy.xml, into ImageMagick's system policy, such as /etc/ImageMagick-7/policy.xml. At a minimum, block the MSL coder, the Ghostscript coders, and the gs delegate. Rails also published the fix as patches for 8.1 and 8.0.

Apps on release series older than 8.0 can use that workaround or upgrade to 8.0 or later.

Rails' workarounds for the second flaw only change how FFmpeg is used. None of them covers ImageMagick.

If the app stores attachments with the Disk service, change secret_key_base and every other secret the app process can read. That includes the master key, everything config/credentials.yml.enc holds, storage and database credentials, and third-party tokens. Do not keep an exposed secret as a fallback.

The advisory does not explain how to check whether an app has already been targeted.

ebf6de35159e.text:
Hunt.io traced ARTEX servers and AI-powered hacking tools used in breaches affecting seven South Korean financial institutions.

Between late September and early October 2026, seven South Korean financial institutions had data breached through internet-facing systems. About 66,000 to 67,000 people and around 2,200 corporations were affected, and personal, employment, income and loan data was exposed. Hunt.io dug into the infrastructure behind the campaign, and its findings add a lot to what CrowdStrike and Genians already published.

CrowdStrike reported on October 7 and Genians Security Center on October 12, and both pointed to ARTEX, an open-source autonomous penetration testing framework developed in China and licensed under AGPL-3.0. CrowdStrike assessed with moderate confidence that a single Chinese-speaking individual motivated by money ran it, and not an established threat group. DeepSeek v4.1 Flash was the main model, with GLM 5.3 and Grok 4.6 as backups, reached partly through a reseller domain, xcai[.]pro.

The public indicators were a server at 38.244.50[.]120, which hosted the ARTEX console, plus a Hong Kong address and nine proxies. Genians said the ARTEX GitHub repository and Docker image were removed on October 11, though forks and mirrors remain.

“CrowdStrike assessed with moderate confidence that the operator was a single Chinese-speaking individual motivated by financial gain rather than an established threat group.” reads the report published by Hunt.io. “The infrastructure reportedly accessed these services in part through the reseller domain xcai[.]pro. Both reports described a two-server configuration, consisting of a Hong Kong-based IP address used as primary infrastructure and 38.244.50[.]120, which hosted the ARTEX console.”

Hunt.io notified the relevant national CERT before publishing, and says the report holds no personal records or credentials.

The company’s own scanning showed 38.244.50[.]120 sits on Cogent’s network in Los Angeles, with 15 open ports. The ARTEX login page, with a Chinese title meaning “autonomous penetration testing console”, appears on ports 443 and 8090. Other services include a Gemini2API admin console and a Tinyproxy server.

Searching its AttackCapture platform for that address, Hunt.io found another open directory at 23.248.226[.]250, a jump server in Hong Kong on AS138415. It held 42 files in 2 subdirectories, 105 MB in all, and the platform had logged warnings on September 5, September 26 and October 5. A file in it names 38.244.50[.]120 as the jump host, and its own comment tells the operator never to paste the credentials into a session. It sat in an open directory.

Three scripts back up the link. They keep reverse SSH tunnels alive, run a local relay, and copy files to the jump host, one tunnel is named grok2api, and the credentials file also holds keys for Zhipu AI’s GLM models, an OpenAI-compatible relay and a proxy service. That explains how several language models ran in one campaign.

The AI setup is the most striking part. A state file shows the harness is Claude Code itself, version 2.1.221, started 510 times since August 4, but it isn’t talking to Anthropic. A small proxy, ds-models-shim.py, fixes a compatibility problem by faking a model list and sending requests to DeepSeek, and another, xcai-effort-shim.py, adds a reasoning setting because the DeepSeek backend otherwise skips its reasoning step. The route runs from Claude Code through Claude Code Router, an open-source project, to xcai and then to DeepSeek.

“A small local proxy, ds-models-shim.py, addresses a compatibility issue: the official /v1/models endpoint returns a 404 response when queried against a non-Anthropic backend, preventing Claude Code from discovering the available models. The shim intercepts that specific request and returns a locally defined model list containing deepseek-v4-pro and deepseek-flash. All other requests are forwarded to api.deepseek.com/anthropic.” states the report.

The same file counts 19 custom skills, reusable instruction sets for the agent, with 147 recorded uses. They cover code audit, reconnaissance, web injection, WAF bypass testing, authentication testing, Telegram Mini Apps, APK download and decompiling, cloud phone control and payment logic testing. Next to the payment skill sat three self-registered test accounts with tokens for a cash-in deposit API, dated September 12, and a comment calls them an authorized, self-built test. The setup fits testing for insecure direct object reference flaws, a technique CrowdStrike and Genians described against Korean loan and inquiry services.

The directory also held supporting tools. A script queried FOFA, a Chinese asset search engine like Shodan, through a third-party API, and a comment says the primary membership had expired and a backup key was in use. Proxy scripts enumerated a rotating proxy service at 154.201.79[.]246:443, where 79 unique exit IPs showed up among the first 100 identities tested.

A separate directory at 23.248.226[.]250:8001 held a small staged setup for JNDI and LDAP exploitation, retrieved on October 5 at 03:42 UTC. It confirms command execution through a DNS callback, and one script lets web and LDAP traffic share a single port. Hunt.io’s analysis describes the tooling without publishing steps to reproduce it.

Other recovered files include tools aimed at a cryptocurrency exchange’s admin session and withdrawals, Linux privilege escalation exploits, iOS probe source code and Android kernel and firmware utilities. Hunt.io says their connection to the Korean breaches isn’t confirmed.

Hunt.io then showed how to hunt ARTEX servers. Searching for an ARTEX certificate issuer returned 19 IP addresses, and searching its malware classification returned 1,303 addresses across 30 countries, led by the United States, China and Hong Kong. Those figures show where addresses are registered, not where the operator sits.

“The result returned 19 distinct IP addresses, including 38.244.50[.]120. This method is precise but limited to hosts that expose a matching certificate. Systems using a different certificate will not appear in these results.” continues the report.

Matching the console’s page title returned about 1,300 IPs, and a looser search found 21 title strings, 19 of them likely ARTEX consoles, in English, Chinese, Korean, Japanese, Russian, Portuguese and Vietnamese.

A malware-name search in AttackCapture gave 280 results with open directories. One at 130.94.31[.]86:18888 in Seoul held two small scripts, and another at 156.251.11[.]39 held an SMB reconnaissance toolkit whose test script writes a file named artex_probe_11876.txt.

More hosts held exploitation kits for DedeCMS and FangCMS, a CAPTCHA bypass suite, a RuoYi and Spring administrative console exploit and CAPTCHA-based login automation. Together they show the framework attracting many operators.

For defenders, the advice is plain. Remove public access and put administration behind VPNs or allowlists, and reset SSH passwords and rotate API keys, proxy credentials and tokens that exposed files may have revealed. Patch internet-facing services, watch for unexpected LDAP and JNDI activity, DNS callbacks and remote script downloads, and store secrets in a managed vault with least-privilege permissions. Also restrict access to model gateways, watch their requests, and enforce compliance rules on managed phones. Hunt.io’s lesson is that an investigation shouldn’t stop at the first list of indicators, because

The company also published indicators of compromise in its analysis.

“The findings highlight risks associated with exposed administrative services, reusable credentials, remote access tunnels, proxy infrastructure, and exploitation tooling.” concludes the report.

e015b06399b8.text:
Software vendors can boost revenue by tracking customer usage across products, while AI accelerates pricing and consumption decisions.

It is hard to find any software vendor that sells just one product. Portfolios have expanded from modules to editions, cloud services, add-ons, and now AI capabilities.

A lot can be achieved through an expanded portfolio. IDC research commissioned by Thales shows that customers with consolidated agreements “spend more, churn less, and deepen their relationship with the vendor over time.”

However, there is one thing to note. Purchasing four products from the same vendor does not mean they will be treated as a single vendor, as each product has its own licensing, measurement, and sales terms.

The Size of the Prize

Existing customers are an obvious place to look for growth. The possible upside could be considerable. According to IDC research on software vendors from June 2026, 55% of software vendors believe that enhanced monetization would bring a 6% to 10% uplift in revenue, and 29% expect more than 10%.

IDC has also linked a SaaS provider’s ability to capitalize systematically on new features and capabilities to net revenue retention and growth. Companies that excel at this see it in their valuations too. McKinsey research shows top-quartile B2B SaaS companies achieve 113% net revenue retention, growing 13% from existing customers alone, against 98% for bottom-quartile peers.

Capturing that opportunity becomes harder when the commercial systems behind the portfolio cannot see across it. Sales teams may know a customer well, but they also need to know what that customer has bought, what they are entitled to use, and how much of it they are consuming. That information is what turns a general cross-sell conversation into a relevant one.

Where Portfolio Revenue Leaks Away

Product launches or acquisitions might occur at different times, and the business units could operate independently. With time, each one may build its own licensing approach, customer database, product catalog, and commercial model.

IDC’s vendor research found that only 25% of software vendors have centralized usage data.

In practice, vendors need to at least unify the entitlement system first. All of the products need to sit in one catalog before the vendor can create a bundled offer across them. Getting there can stall for technical, organizational, or budget reasons.

But the reason to overcome those barriers comes back to the customer experience. A company may be optimized internally around separate product lines or business units, while customers still have to go to multiple places to access and manage products they bought from the same vendor.

Customer pressure has historically forced companies to restructure and centralize around that problem. Licensing and entitlement ownership can move out of individual product lines and into a central function, such as engineering operations, product operations, supply chain operations, or SaaS operations. For that to work, the central function needs real authority rather than existing in name only.

A customer could be approaching the limits of Product A while another part of the company sells Product B, which would be a logical next purchase. The usage data contains the signal, but it may sit in a system that the team responsible for Product B never sees.

AI can multiply this problem quickly. Vendors no longer need to launch an entirely new application before they have something new to monetize. A new model, agent, workflow, or premium feature could all require decisions about entitlements, usage, and price.

Over time, however, customers can end up with a growing collection of meters, contract terms, entitlements, and invoice lines. The vendor sees one expanding portfolio. The customer sees the work required to understand and manage it.

Buyers are already feeling this pressure. IDC’s customer research found that 45% struggle to reconcile purchased licenses with actual usage, while 39% cite inflexible licensing models as a challenge. At the same time, 60% of buyers report an active drive to reduce the number of software vendors they use.

Consolidating with a strategic supplier becomes much less attractive if it leaves the customer managing the same complexity under a single company name.

What Unified Portfolio Monetization Enables

A shared entitlement system brings products from different business units into one catalog, giving vendors a consistent view of what customers have bought and what they can use. That common foundation is what makes portfolio-wide bundles and offers possible.

Vendors do not necessarily have to wait for every commercial system to be consolidated before they get there. Thales can bring third-party license generators onto one platform, while Central Migrate and Thales’s internal migration expertise and best practices support the move from existing licensing systems.

Shared credits or pooled consumption can provide another option. Customers have a single balance that can be used across multiple products or capabilities. As vendors add AI features with different consumption patterns, this gives them room to introduce new capabilities without automatically introducing a standalone commercial model for each.

M&A Creates Another Portfolio Opportunity

The same issue appears after an acquisition. CEOs are looking for the “1+1=3” outcome: creating more value from the combined business than the two companies could separately.

The acquirer can sell its portfolio to the acquired company’s customers, while the acquired company’s products can be introduced to the acquirer’s customer base.

The problem is that full M&A integration can take time, particularly when ERP and ordering systems are involved. Entitlement systems can be unified much sooner and with considerably less work than a full ordering-system integration.

That allows portfolio monetization to run in parallel with the heavier systems work rather than waiting for it to finish. The business can start cross-selling across the combined customer base sooner, giving leadership a way to demonstrate acquisition ROI faster.

Turning Usage Into Expansion Opportunities

Usage data then becomes useful beyond billing. Vendors can see which customers own Product A but not Product B, which customers are consuming, and which customers are regularly reaching the limits of their current entitlement.

They can also change the renewal conversation. Actual consumption provides a much stronger basis for discussing the next contract than assumptions made when the previous agreement was signed. It shows what customers are using heavily, what they are barely touching, and where there may be a natural opportunity for upselling and cross-selling.

Buyers appear open to this kind of consolidation. IDC found that 86% are somewhat and extremely interested in a single licensing agreement covering multiple products from the same vendor. Runaway costs are the biggest concern around vendor consolidation, cited by 74%, followed by lack of flexibility at 62% and lack of transparency at 59%.

Those concerns put some useful boundaries around portfolio monetization. Bringing more products into one commercial relationship needs to make them easier for the customer to understand and manage. Visibility into consumption, clear entitlements, and controls over spend become more important as the portfolio grows.

Making a Larger Portfolio Easier to Buy

AI is likely to keep adding features, agents, models, and new forms of consumption to software portfolios.

Portfolio growth works better when the entitlement system cuts across product and business-unit silos. Customers can see what they own, understand what they are consuming, and use more of the vendor’s products without having to navigate a new commercial process each time.

The IDC report shows that buyers already want greater flexibility, visibility, and control. The opportunity for vendors is to make expansion across the portfolio easier to buy and manage, even as the underlying technology becomes more complex.

About the Author: Manoj Tharakan is Director of Product Management, CDI, at Thales, where he works on software licensing, SaaS billing, and monetization. With over 20 years across software licensing, SaaS billing, and monetization, he’s helped build the systems vendors rely on to actually get paid for the value they create.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, AI)

Security operations startup Brava Security has emerged from stealth mode with $15 million in a seed funding round led by F2 Venture Capital and Pitango VC, with support from several angel investors.

Tel Aviv-based Brava was founded in 2024 by Israeli intelligence alumni Idan Basre, who serves as CEO, and Itay Gabbay, the company’s CTO.

Brava has built an AI-powered platform that focuses on modeling attacker behavior, simulating attacks to analyze generated telemetry for security gaps.

Using business context, the solution shows how an attack would manifest in customers’ environments, reveals what defenses could miss, and rewrites SIEM detections, while allowing security teams to investigate further.

“The hard part of security was never writing detections. It’s knowing exactly what an attack will look like in a specific environment, across all of its log sources, before it ever happens. That’s the problem our models were built to solve,” said Gabbay.

Brava says this approach closes an important gap in modern security defenses, since AI agents typically cannot investigate attacks their systems haven’t detected.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

“You can’t automate a decision based on evidence no one ever proved. We’re solving the problem that comes before AI can make the right decision: making sure the security infrastructure actually sees the threats it’s supposed to detect,” Basre said.

According to Brava, its platform can provide initial insights within 10-15 minutes of onboarding. The solution integrates with more than 70 sources and destinations and does not require changes to existing security infrastructure.

The startup will use the fresh funding to accelerate product development and market expansion. It currently has an R&D team in Israel and a commercial team in the US.

French Bank Crédit Mutuel Arkéa says hackers exploited a service provider to steal up to $133 million using the bank’s own account.

French cooperative bank Crédit Mutuel Arkéa was hit by a cyberattack that let attackers make fraudulent transactions of up to $133 million, forcing it to suspend certain systems. Crédit Mutuel Arkéa is a major French cooperative banking and insurance group headquartered in Brest, Brittany, France.

The bank says the attacker used its own account to send transactions to other banking organizations, and that customer assets weren’t affected.

“French lender Credit Mutuel Arkea said on Thursday hackers had stolen around €100 million ($112.61 million) in a cyber heist and it was working to try to recover the money, in a rare case of cybercriminals successfully stealing from a mainstream bank.” Reuters states.

Blockchain researcher ZachXBT first warned of a large unauthorized withdrawal from multiple centralized exchange accounts a day earlier. He said the attacker may have stolen up to 118 million euros ($133 million) and withdrawn it as the USDC and USDT stablecoins.

“Over the past 24 hours the illicit actor has been aggressively swapping USDC for ETH, transferring to instant exchanges (WellWallet, Kyrrex, etc), converting to XMR via Wagyu, and bridging across multiple chains.” ZachXBT wrote.

“While the illicit actor remains unidentified, I can say with a high degree of confidence it is NOT Lazarus Group based on multiple laundering indicators.”

The attacker remains unidentified, but ZachXBT believes it is highly unlikely to be Lazarus Group, based on money-laundering patterns.

According to BleepingComputer, the expert pointed out that the lack of public disclosure allowed attackers to launder $30 million by November 3, potentially preventing EU authorities from freezing the funds. The Paris prosecutor’s cybercrime unit opened an investigation after receiving a complaint from Crédit Mutuel Arkéa, with France’s cybercrime police leading the probe.

Arkéa disclosed the incident on November 4, saying it was contained, customer assets were unaffected and some transfers had been delayed. Attackers reportedly accessed the bank through a service provider’s platform, not Fortuneo, and used Arkéa’s own account to move funds through other banks and convert them into cryptocurrency. The bank also warned customers about increased phishing risks.

“Crédit Mutuel Arkéa announces that it has been the target of an attack that enabled the execution of fraudulent transactions.” reads the notice published by the bank. “Upon detecting this attack, and in accordance with standard procedures, the Group contacted the relevant regulatory and supervisory authorities to inform them of the situation.” “This incident is now closed and fully under control. Operations are gradually resuming this morning, following thorough verification by the Group and its subsidiaries and the implementation of enhanced security measures.”

Crédit Mutuel Arkéa says customer assets were unaffected, although some transfers were delayed. The bank maintains its financial stability, warns of possible phishing attempts and urges customers not to share sensitive information. Its teams are assessing the incident and strengthening security measures, with further updates expected.

Arkéa did not confirm ZachXBT’s reported figure but acknowledged significant losses and said some funds were blocked. The bank ruled out internal human error, described the incident as a sophisticated attack and is working with law enforcement to identify the attackers and establish how the breach occurred.

When the FAQ asked whether 118 million euros had been stolen, Arkéa wouldn’t give a number: We do not confirm this information and can only validate the order of magnitude.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Crédit Mutuel Arkéa)
